subject: rla
title: Analyzing Arguments: Claims, Evidence, Reasoning, and Faulty Reasoning
objectives: You will identify an author's claim, reasons, counterclaim, and rebuttal in an argument.
You will classify evidence and judge whether it is relevant, sufficient, and reliable.
You will explain how reasoning connects evidence to a claim and find the unstated assumption.
You will recognize faulty reasoning: hasty generalization, false cause, slippery slope, either-or, attack on the person, bandwagon, straw man, and appeal to emotion.
You will judge the credibility of sources (Who, What, When, Why) and decide what would strengthen or weaken an argument.

slides.title: Analyzing Arguments: Claims, Evidence, Reasoning, and Faulty Reasoning
slides.board:
Week 5 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Find the claim, reasons, counterclaim, and rebuttal
  • Test evidence: relevant, sufficient, reliable
  • Spot the hidden assumption
  • Name eight kinds of faulty reasoning
  • Judge sources and what strengthens or weakens an argument

Plan: Warm-up · Learn and practice together · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: Welcome to week 5. Today we take arguments apart and judge how well they hold up. A big share of GED reading passages are arguments: op-eds, letters to the editor, speeches, position papers. The extended response is built entirely on this skill, because you will have to decide which of two arguments is better supported. One rule for the whole hour: we never decide which side is right. We decide which side proves its point.
ask: Think of the last time someone tried to convince you of something, an ad, a post, a friend. Did they prove it, or just say it? (expected: any honest example; use it later as a running example)

slides.title: Review: word meaning and tone
slides.board:
Last week's skills. Answer out loud.

  1. “The council's frugal budget cut every extra, down to the paper clips.” What does frugal mean?
  2. Positive or negative? thrifty · cheap
  3. “The proposal was a train wreck from the first page.” What kind of language is this, and what does it mean?
  4. Name the tone: “Once again, the board has bravely decided to do nothing.”
steps: 1. Careful with money; spending as little as possible. Clue: “cut every extra, down to the paper clips.”
2. Thrifty is positive; cheap is negative. Same denotation, different connotation.
3. A metaphor: the proposal was a disaster from the start.
4. Sarcastic: “bravely” praises the board on the surface, but “do nothing” shows the writer means the opposite.

notes.say: This warm-up reviews week 4, and every question connects to today. Word choice matters in arguments: writers pick words with strong connotations to push readers, and today we will call that loaded language. Give about a minute for each question. Ask for the clue in the sentence, not just the answer.
notes.answer: 1. Careful with money, spending as little as possible (example clue). 2. Thrifty: positive; cheap: negative. 3. Metaphor; the proposal was a complete failure. 4. Sarcastic (also accept mocking or critical), because the praise word clashes with “do nothing.”
notes.watch: If the student struggles with connotation (question 2), slow down. Today's “loaded language” and “appeal to emotion” depend on noticing when a word carries a feeling the facts do not.

slides.title: Which one convinces you?
slides.board:
A: We need a fenced dog park downtown. Everybody knows dogs need exercise, and anyone who disagrees just doesn't like dogs.

B: We need a fenced dog park downtown. The city licensing office reports 2,300 licensed dogs within one mile of Main Street, and the nearest fenced dog area is four miles away.

Which is more convincing? Give one specific reason.
steps: Same claim in both: we need a fenced dog park downtown.
A's support: “everybody knows” (not evidence) and an insult to people who disagree.
B's support: specific numbers from a named office a reader could check, and they connect to the claim (many dogs, no nearby park).
B is better supported. You can agree with a claim and still see that it is poorly supported.

notes.say: Both statements make the same claim, so the only difference is the support. That is the whole lesson in miniature. Let the student pick and explain before you reveal anything. If they say “B has numbers,” push further: numbers from where, and do they connect to the claim?
ask: Could someone who does not own a dog still admit that B is better supported? (expected: yes; support is about proof, not about whether you like the idea)
notes.answer: B. It uses checkable numbers from the city licensing office that connect directly to the claim. A relies on “everybody knows” and attacks the people who disagree.

slides.title: The parts of an argument
slides.board:
PartQuestion it answers
ClaimWhat does the author want me to believe or do?
ReasonWhy, according to the author?
EvidenceWhat proves each reason?
CounterclaimWhat does the other side say?
RebuttalHow does the author answer it?

Claim test: Could a reasonable person disagree? “The library closes at 6” is a fact. “The library should stay open until 9” is a claim.

notes.say: An argument is writing that tries to convince you to believe or do something. Every argument has a claim, and good arguments back the claim with reasons and evidence. Stronger arguments also face the other side: they state a counterclaim and answer it with a rebuttal. The claim is usually near the start and repeated at the end. Signal words help: should, must, need to often mark a claim; some people say, critics argue mark a counterclaim; but, however, yet often start the rebuttal.
ask: Fact or claim: “The bus fare is $2.” (expected: fact)
Fact or claim: “The bus fare should be lowered for seniors.” (expected: claim; people could disagree)
notes.watch: Students often call a striking statistic the claim. Ask: “Is this what the author wants us to do, or proof of it?”

slides.title: Find the parts
slides.board:
(1) The library should open on Sunday afternoons. (2) Many students work on Saturdays and have no quiet place to study on weekends. (3) When the library tested Sunday hours last spring, an average of 210 people came each Sunday. (4) Some say the library cannot afford more hours. (5) However, the library director reports that a literacy grant already covers the cost of staff for those hours.

Label each sentence.
steps: Sentence 1, claim: what the writer wants (“should open”).
Sentence 2, reason: why (students need weekend study space).
Sentence 3, evidence: a number from a real trial (210 people each Sunday).
Sentence 4, counterclaim: “Some say” signals the other side.
Sentence 5, rebuttal: “However” answers the cost worry with the director's report.

notes.say: Model this out loud, one sentence at a time. Start with the claim because everything else is defined by its job toward the claim. Then ask of each sentence: does it give a reason, prove a reason, give the other side, or answer the other side?
ask: Which word told you sentence 4 is the other side? (expected: “Some say”)

slides.title: Label it together
slides.board:
(1) The town should add a Sunday farmers market from June through September. (2) Right now the market runs only on Saturday mornings, when many residents are working. (3) Last fall, 30 of the market's 42 vendors said they would sell on Sundays too. (4) Some people say a second day will split the crowd and hurt Saturday sales. (5) But in nearby Oakdale, Saturday attendance has stayed steady since its Sunday market opened.

Claim? Counterclaim? Rebuttal? What kind of evidence is sentence 3?
steps: Claim: sentence 1 (“should add”).
Counterclaim: sentence 4 (“Some people say”).
Rebuttal: sentence 5 (“But” + Oakdale's steady attendance).
Sentence 3 is statistics from a survey of vendors. It is relevant: a market needs vendors willing to come on Sunday.

notes.say: Now the student leads and you guide. Ask for each part, and reveal a step only after the student answers it. Ask them to name the signal word each time; that habit is what makes this fast on the test.
ask: Is sentence 2 evidence or a reason? (expected: a reason; it explains why, but gives no numbers or source)
notes.watch: If the student calls sentence 5 evidence, agree that it contains evidence, then ask what job it does: it answers sentence 4, so its role is rebuttal.

slides.title: Evidence: kinds and three tests
slides.board:
Kinds: statistics · research studies · expert statements · comparable cases · anecdotes (personal stories) · personal observation

TestAsk
RelevantIs it about this claim?
SufficientIs there enough to cover the size of the claim?
ReliableWhere did it come from? Was it gathered fairly? Could I check it?

notes.say: Evidence is the proof. Not all proof is equal, so we test every piece three ways. Relevant: a true fact about the wrong subject does not help. Sufficient: one story cannot prove something about a whole town. Reliable: a named source with fair methods beats a rumor or a poll where people chose themselves. Anecdotes are not wrong; they make an argument vivid. But by themselves, they are weak support for a big claim.
ask: A claim is about the whole county. The evidence is one family's story. Which test does it fail? (expected: sufficient)
notes.watch: Students often think any number is strong evidence. Ask how the number was gathered and who was counted.

slides.title: Test the evidence
slides.board:
Claim: The county should add a second ambulance station on the east side.

  1. County records show average ambulance response time on the east side is 14 minutes, compared with 7 minutes elsewhere.
  2. My neighbor waited what felt like forever for an ambulance last year.
  3. Ambulances in the county were painted a brighter yellow in 2022.

Run the three tests on each.
steps: 1: relevant (east-side response times), sufficient (covers many calls), reliable (county records). Strong.
2: relevant, but one story is not sufficient, and “what felt like forever” is not measured, so it is not reliable.
3: true, perhaps, but not relevant: paint color says nothing about the need for a station.
Best support: evidence 1.

notes.say: Walk through each piece of evidence with all three tests. The point is that each weak piece fails for a different reason, and the GED wants students to say why evidence is weak, not just that it is.
ask: Which test does evidence 3 fail? (expected: relevant)

slides.title: Which evidence is strongest?
slides.board:
Claim: Our high school should start classes at 8:30 instead of 7:30.

  1. A survey of 40 students in one first-period gym class
  2. A study of 9,000 students in eight school districts that moved start times later and tracked attendance and grades
  3. A teacher's comment that students “look tired”
  4. The number of students who play fall sports

Rank the evidence from strongest to weakest.
steps: Strongest: 2. Large, many districts, measured results, directly about later start times.
Next: 1. Relevant, but 40 students in one class is not sufficient for a whole school.
Then: 3. One person's impression; not measured, not sufficient.
Weakest: 4. Not relevant to start times as given.

notes.say: Let the student rank first, then reveal one step at a time. Ask for the test each weak piece fails. There can be some debate between the weakest two; what matters is the reason.
ask: Why is evidence 1 weaker than evidence 2 if both are about students? (expected: too few students, one class, not sufficient)
notes.answer: 2, 1, 3, 4. Accept 2, 3, 1, 4 if the student explains that the survey and the comment are both too small. Evidence 4 is weakest because it is not relevant.
notes.watch: If a student ranks the teacher's comment first “because teachers know,” point out that expertise helps, but an impression with no measurement is still weak.

slides.title: Reasoning and hidden assumptions
slides.board:
Evidence → reasoning → claim

Reasoning is the bridge. An assumption is a part of the bridge the author does not say out loud.

Ask: “What must be true for this evidence to prove this claim?”

Weak assumption = weak argument.

notes.say: Evidence does not prove anything by itself. The writer has to connect it to the claim, and often part of that connection is unstated. To find the assumption, ask what must be true for the evidence to lead to the claim. A very common assumption on the GED is that one place, group, or time is like another: what worked over there will work here.
ask: “Gym members who take spin classes lose more weight, so spin classes cause weight loss.” What is assumed? (expected: that the spin class, not something else about those members, caused the weight loss)

slides.title: Find the assumption
slides.board:
“Our town should keep the pool open until 8 p.m. In a survey of 900 pass holders, 64 percent said they would swim more often with evening hours. Neighboring Westbrook extended its hours and sold 20 percent more season passes the next summer, which paid for the extra lifeguard shifts.”

What must be true for the Westbrook evidence to prove the claim?
steps: Evidence: Westbrook's longer hours led to more pass sales.
Claim: our town should do the same.
Assumption: our town is similar enough to Westbrook that pass sales would rise here too and cover the cost.
Judge it: reasonable but unproven. The writer never gives our own cost of extra shifts, so the money part is not fully supported.

notes.say: Model the bridge. First name the evidence and the claim, then say out loud what would have to be true to cross from one to the other. Then judge whether that assumption is safe.
ask: What fact would make this assumption stronger? (expected: our town and Westbrook have similar size, weather, or demand; or the survey of our own pass holders shows demand)

slides.title: Faulty reasoning, part 1: weak links
slides.board:
TypeWhat it doesAsk
Hasty generalizationBig conclusion from too few casesEnough examples?
False causeB came after A, so A caused BWhat else could explain it?
Slippery slopeOne step leads to a chain of disastersIs each step proven?
Either-orOnly two choices when more existAre there other options?

notes.say: Faulty reasoning, also called a logical fallacy, makes an argument seem stronger than it is. These first four are problems with the link between evidence and conclusion. A hasty generalization stretches a few cases too far. False cause treats timing as proof. A slippery slope predicts a chain of bad results without proving each step. Either-or pretends there are only two choices. Ask the student for an everyday example of each.
ask: “I got sick the day after my flu shot, so the shot made me sick.” Which type? (expected: false cause)
notes.watch: The GED rarely asks for the name of a fallacy. It asks which reasoning is flawed or which statement is not supported. The names are tools for spotting flaws fast.

slides.title: Faulty reasoning, part 2: dodging the issue
slides.board:
TypeWhat it doesAsk
Attack on the personCriticizes the people, not their reasonsWere the reasons answered?
BandwagonIt is right because many people do itIs popular the same as proven?
Straw manTwists the other side's view into a weaker oneDid they really say that?
Appeal to emotionFeelings or loaded words replace evidenceRemove the emotion: what proof is left?

notes.say: These four avoid the real question. An attack on the person goes after who someone is instead of what they said. Bandwagon treats popularity as proof. A straw man defeats a fake, weaker version of the other side. An appeal to emotion uses fear, pity, or loaded words instead of evidence. Stress that emotion is not a flaw by itself; a moving story next to solid data is fine. It becomes a flaw when it is the only support.
ask: “Critics of the curfew want teenagers roaming the streets all night with no rules at all.” Which type? (expected: straw man)
notes.watch: Remind the student that every side of every issue uses these. If an example seems to target one political side, swap in one from the other side.

slides.title: Name the flaw
slides.board:
1. “Speeding tickets went up after the new coffee shop opened. That shop is causing reckless driving.”
  2. “If seniors can leave campus for lunch, next they will skip whole afternoons, and soon no one will be in class.”
  3. “Ms. Park wants bike lanes, but she can't even keep her own yard tidy.”
  4. “Either we raise the library budget, or our children will grow up unable to read.”
  5. “My cousin's car was broken into downtown, so downtown is not safe.”
steps: 1. False cause: tickets rose after the shop opened, but more traffic or more patrols could explain it.
2. Slippery slope: no proof that a lunch policy leads to empty classrooms.
3. Attack on the person: her yard has nothing to do with bike lanes.
4. Either-or: there are many ways to support reading besides this one budget.
5. Hasty generalization: one break-in cannot show a whole area is unsafe.

notes.say: Model the thinking for each: what is the conclusion, what is the proof, and where does the link break? Then name the pattern. Notice that these come from different points of view; faulty reasoning is a habit of thinking, not a feature of one side.
ask: For number 5, what evidence would actually show whether downtown is safe? (expected: crime data for downtown over time, compared with other areas)

slides.title: Flaw hunt together
slides.board:
(1) The city should not build the new transit center on Grove Street. (2) The planning office estimates the project will close two lanes of Grove Street for eighteen months. (3) Everyone in my building is against it, so the city should listen. (4) Supporters of the project just want to see their names on a plaque. (5) If the city builds this, buses will clog every street downtown, businesses will flee, and the city will be a ghost town.

Which sentences are faulty reasoning? Which is real support?
steps: Sentence 2: real support. An estimate from a named office, relevant to the cost of the project.
Sentence 3: bandwagon (and too few people to speak for a city).
Sentence 4: attack on the person; it judges supporters' motives, not their reasons.
Sentence 5: slippery slope with loaded language (“ghost town”); no step is proven.

notes.say: The student leads. For each sentence, ask: is this proof about the transit center, or something else? Reveal a step only after the student commits. Point out that a writer can use both sound evidence and faulty reasoning in the same letter.
ask: Is sentence 1 faulty reasoning? (expected: no; it is the claim)
notes.answer: Sentence 1: claim. Sentence 2: sound, relevant evidence. Sentence 3: bandwagon (also a hasty generalization). Sentence 4: attack on the person. Sentence 5: slippery slope with appeal to emotion.
notes.watch: If the student labels sentence 2 as faulty “because it is negative,” remind them that a fact can hurt one side and still be good evidence.

slides.title: Judging a source: Who, What, When, Why
slides.board:
Ask
WhoDoes the author have real knowledge of the subject?
WhatData and methods I could check, or just opinion?
WhenIs it current for this question?
WhyDoes the author gain money, votes, or customers if I agree?

Credible and relevant are two separate tests. Check both.

notes.say: Credibility is how far we can trust a source. Four questions cover it. A source with a stake in the outcome is not automatically wrong, but we look harder at its evidence. And a very credible source can still be off target: a strong study of other cities does not prove what happened on one street in our city.
ask: A sunscreen company's website says its product prevents sunburn better than any other. Which question raises the biggest concern? (expected: Why; the company profits if you believe it)
notes.watch: Students sometimes treat “older” as “more reliable” or treat any expert as automatically right. Ask: is it current, and is it about this exact question?

slides.title: Which source is most credible?
slides.board:
Question: Do standing desks reduce back pain for office workers?

  1. A standing-desk company's website, 2025: “Our customers report 90 percent less back pain!”
  2. A 2023 medical-journal study: university researchers followed 400 office workers for a year, comparing standing-desk users with non-users.
  3. A 2008 magazine article on office furniture trends.
  4. A video by a fitness personality who says standing desks “changed my life.”
steps: Source 1: profits from sales (Why); “customers report” is not a fair study (What).
Source 3: old (When) and about trends, not health (What).
Source 4: one person's experience (What), not sufficient.
Source 2 is most credible: trained researchers, 400 workers with a comparison group, recent, published to share findings.

notes.say: Run Who, What, When, Why on each source out loud. Emphasize the comparison group in source 2; comparing users with non-users is what makes the result meaningful.
ask: Why does the comparison group matter? (expected: it shows whether the desks made the difference, not just time or other changes)

slides.title: Strengthen or weaken?
slides.board:
Strengthens: new evidence that makes the claim more likely, often by supporting the assumption.

Weakens: new evidence that breaks the link between the proof and the claim, often by attacking the assumption.

Method: 1. Find the claim. 2. Find the key evidence. 3. Name the assumption. 4. Ask what each choice does to that assumption.

notes.say: The GED often asks “Which statement, if true, would most weaken the argument?” Students should accept each choice as true and ask what it does to the argument. The fastest route is through the assumption: whatever the argument takes for granted is where it can break. A choice that repeats evidence already in the passage or talks about a different issue does not change the argument.
ask: If an argument assumes our town is like Westbrook, what kind of fact would weaken it? (expected: a fact showing the two towns are very different)

slides.title: Strengthen or weaken: free parking
slides.board:
Claim: The town should replace downtown parking meters with free two-hour parking, because free parking will bring more shoppers to downtown stores.

(a) In three nearby towns that removed meters, downtown store sales rose the next year.

(b) In a survey of downtown shoppers, most said their biggest problem was finding an open space, not paying for one.

(c) Downtown parking meters were installed in 1987.
steps: Assumption: the cost of parking keeps shoppers away.
(a) Strengthens: the expected result happened in comparable towns.
(b) Weakens: if cost is not the problem, free parking may not help, and free spaces may fill faster.
(c) Neither: the age of the meters says nothing about shoppers.

notes.say: Name the assumption first: cost is what keeps shoppers away. Then test each fact against it. Point out that choice (c) is a classic distractor: true-sounding, on topic, but it changes nothing.
ask: What could the writer add to answer fact (b)? (expected: a time limit or turnover plan, or data showing open spaces would not shrink)

slides.title: Your turn: parts and evidence
slides.board:
1. (1) The city should add more trash cans along the river trail. (2) Volunteers removed 1,100 pounds of litter from the trail last spring. (3) Some argue that more cans just mean more cans to empty. (4) Yet the parks department says emptying costs less than the twice-yearly cleanups. Label claim, evidence, counterclaim, rebuttal.

2. Claim: “Our county needs more child care centers.” Which evidence is strongest? (a) “My sister can't find a spot.” (b) State data: the county has 1 licensed child care slot for every 4 children under 5. (c) “Child care matters to everyone.”
steps: 1. Claim 1 · evidence 2 · counterclaim 3 · rebuttal 4.
2. (b): relevant, sufficient (covers the county), reliable (state data). (a) is one story; (c) is a general statement with no proof.

notes.say: Start a four-minute timer and stay quiet while the student works. When time is up, have them give each answer with a reason before you reveal.
notes.answer: 1. Sentence 1 claim (“should add”); sentence 2 evidence (measured litter); sentence 3 counterclaim (“Some argue”); sentence 4 rebuttal (“Yet” + parks department). 2. (b). (a) fails sufficient; (c) is not evidence at all.
notes.watch: If the student calls sentence 2 the claim because it has a big number, return to the claim test: is this something people could disagree about, or proof of something?

slides.title: Your turn: name the flaw
slides.board:
Name the faulty reasoning.

  1. “Millions of people use this sleep app, so it must improve sleep.”
  2. “Two of my coworkers got sick after eating at the new taco stand. Its food is unsafe.”
  3. “Either we cut the summer reading program or we raise property taxes.”
  4. “My opponent wants to raise the speed limit. Clearly, he doesn't care if children get hurt.”
steps: 1. Bandwagon: popularity is not proof it works.
2. Hasty generalization (also possible false cause): two cases cannot prove the food is unsafe.
3. Either-or: grants, donations, or other cuts are possible.
4. Attack on the person plus straw man: it judges the opponent's character and twists his position.

notes.say: Give three minutes. Ask the student to say what question they would ask the writer for each one; that question is the real skill.
notes.answer: 1. Bandwagon. 2. Hasty generalization (accept false cause if the student explains that the illness came after the meal but other causes are possible). 3. Either-or. 4. Attack on the person; accept straw man if explained.
notes.watch: Some items fit two labels. On the GED you will not need the label; accept any label the student can justify, and focus on the explanation of the flaw.

slides.title: Your turn: sources and weakening
slides.board:
1. Question: Did the city's new recycling program reduce landfill trash? Which source is more credible? (a) The contractor's newsletter: “Our program is a huge success!” (b) The public works report with landfill weights two years before and two years after.

2. Claim: “The school should adopt the new reading software, because a nearby district that used it saw reading scores rise.” Which fact would most weaken it? (a) The nearby district also hired ten reading tutors that year. (b) The software costs $30 per student.
steps: 1. (b): measured weights before and after, from the department that tracks them; (a) has a money stake and no numbers.
2. (a): the tutors could explain the rise, which breaks the assumption that the software caused it. (b) is a cost fact; it does not touch whether the software works.

notes.say: Give three minutes and stay quiet while the student works. For problem 2, remind the student to name the assumption first: what does the argument take for granted? Then have them test each fact against it before you reveal anything.
notes.answer: 1. (b), the public works report. 2. (a), because it gives another cause for the higher scores (the argument assumed the software was the cause).
notes.watch: On problem 2, students often pick the cost fact because it sounds like a reason not to buy. Ask: does it show the software did not work? It does not.

slides.title: GED question: unsupported claim
slides.board:
(1) Our town should hire two more crossing guards for Lincoln Elementary. (2) Police counted 46 near-misses with cars at the Lincoln crosswalks last school year. (3) The district's safety office found that schools with crossing guards at every corner had half as many near-misses. (4) Every parent in town wants this. (5) The cost, $28,000 a year, is less than 0.5 percent of the district's transportation budget.

Which sentence states an idea that is NOT supported by evidence?

A. Sentence 2   B. Sentence 3   C. Sentence 4   D. Sentence 5
steps: A is supported: police counted the near-misses (named source, measured).
B is supported: a finding from the district's safety office.
D is supported: a specific cost compared with the budget.
C is correct: “Every parent in town wants this” has no survey or source, and “every” is far too broad. It is a bandwagon claim.

notes.say: Treat this like the real test. The student should check each sentence for a source or a measurement. Then eliminate together, saying why each supported sentence is supported.
ask: Before you look at the choices, which sentence has no source or number? (expected: sentence 4)
notes.answer: C (sentence 4). Sentences 2, 3, and 5 each give measured information from a named or checkable source.

slides.title: GED question: weaken the argument
slides.board:
“The city should keep the downtown library branch open on Saturdays. When the branch added Saturday hours last year, the number of library cards issued in the city rose by 12 percent.”

Which statement, if true, would most weaken the argument?

A. The library has offered Saturday story time for children since 2015.
B. Last year the city also began giving every new high school student a free library card at enrollment.
C. Saturday is the busiest day for most stores downtown.
D. The downtown branch has more computers than any other branch in the city.
steps: A is not relevant to the 12 percent rise; story time existed long before.
C is about stores, not the library; it does not touch the link.
D describes the branch; it does not explain the rise in cards.
B is correct: free cards for every new high school student offer another cause for the rise, so the Saturday hours may not explain it (false cause).

notes.say: Have the student name the assumption before reading the choices: the Saturday hours caused the rise in library cards. Then test each choice against that assumption.
ask: What does the argument assume? (expected: Saturday hours caused the rise in library cards)
notes.answer: B. It gives an alternate explanation for the increase in library cards, which weakens the assumed cause-and-effect link.

slides.title: GED question: best source
slides.board:
A student asks: Did the four-day school week in Pine County change student attendance?

A. A 2025 Pine County school district report comparing attendance records for three years before and two years after the change, with full data
B. A 2024 national survey of parents' opinions about four-day weeks in general
C. A post by a Pine County bus driver who says “the kids seem happier”
D. A 2018 newspaper article in which the superintendent predicted attendance would improve
steps: B is not specific: national opinions, not Pine County attendance records.
C is one person's impression and about happiness, not attendance.
D is a prediction made before the change, not a result.
A is correct: measured attendance for Pine County before and after, recent, with data a reader can check.

notes.say: Run Who, What, When, Why, and keep the exact question in front of the student: Pine County, attendance, after the change.
ask: Why is D weak even though a superintendent is an expert? (expected: it is a prediction from before the change, not evidence of what happened)
notes.answer: A. It is the only source that measures attendance in Pine County before and after the change.

slides.title: GED strategy: Cover the opinion, check the proof
slides.board:
1. Set your opinion aside. The question is about support, not who is right.
  2. Find the claim first (often first and last paragraphs).
  3. For each answer choice, ask: “Can I point to the proof?”
  4. If the “proof” is one story, a popularity count, an insult, or a prediction, it is weak.
  5. On weaken/strengthen questions, name the assumption before reading the choices.

notes.say: The biggest trap on argument questions is choosing the answer you agree with. Test writers know this. Teach the student to cover their own opinion and look only for proof. This also prepares them for the extended response, where the stronger argument is the better-supported one, even if it is the side they disagree with.
ask: Why can agreeing with the author be a problem on the test? (expected: you may accept weak proof because you like the conclusion)

slides.title: Recap and next steps
slides.board:
• Argument = claim + reasons + evidence; strong ones answer a counterclaim with a rebuttal.
  • Test evidence: relevant, sufficient, reliable.
  • Find the assumption: what must be true for the proof to work?
  • Eight flaws: hasty generalization, false cause, slippery slope, either-or, attack on the person, bandwagon, straw man, appeal to emotion.
  • Sources: Who, What, When, Why; credible is not the same as relevant.

notes.say: Have the student name the three evidence tests and as many flaws as they can from memory before you reveal the recap. Then walk through what comes next: the Student Lesson reviews today step by step with checks, Practice Set A has 15 GED-style questions with the reasoning behind every wrong answer, and the Exit Check confirms they are ready for week 6, where we compare two texts on the same topic.

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Every day, people try to convince you of something: a letter to the editor, a campaign flyer, an ad, a post from a neighbor. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, many passages are arguments like these, and the extended response asks you to decide which of two arguments is better supported. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • find an author's claim, reasons, counterclaim, and rebuttal
  • test evidence: is it relevant, sufficient, and reliable?
  • find the hidden assumption that links evidence to a claim
  • recognize eight kinds of faulty reasoning
  • judge sources and decide what would strengthen or weaken an argument

One rule for the whole lesson: your job is never to decide who is right. Your job is to decide whether the author proves the point. Work one screen at a time. Most screens end with a check you must answer before you move on, and if you miss it, you will see exactly why.

screens.title: What is a claim?
screens.html:
An argument is writing that tries to convince you to believe or do something. Its center is the claim: what the author wants you to believe or do.

The claim test: Could a reasonable person disagree? If yes, it is a claim. If it can simply be checked and is true or false, it is a fact.

“The pool closes at 6 p.m.” is a fact; you can check it. “The pool should stay open until 8 p.m.” is a claim; people could disagree. Claims often use words such as should, must, need to, ought to, or it is time to. The claim usually appears near the beginning of an argument and comes back near the end.

check.prompt:
(1) The town's recycling center is open on Tuesdays and Saturdays. (2) The town should open the recycling center on Sunday afternoons as well. (3) Many residents work on Saturdays and cannot drop off recycling during the week.

Which sentence is the claim? Type the sentence number.
check.hint: Look for the sentence that says what should happen, something people could disagree about.
check.explain: Sentence 2 uses should and states what the writer wants: Sunday hours. People could disagree, so it passes the claim test. Sentence 1 is a checkable fact, and sentence 3 is a reason that supports the claim. Answer: 2.

mistakes.why: Sentence 1 is a fact: you can check the center's hours. No one could reasonably disagree with it. A claim says what should happen.
Sentence 3 is a reason: it explains why the writer wants Sunday hours. The claim is the sentence that says what should happen.

screens.title: Reasons, counterclaims, and rebuttals
screens.html:
A strong argument has more than a claim. It has:

PartJobSignal words
ReasonSays why the claim is rightbecause, first, another reason
EvidenceProves a reasonaccording to, a study found, records show
CounterclaimStates the other sidesome argue, critics say, opponents claim
RebuttalAnswers the other sidehowever, but, yet, in fact

Including a counterclaim does not weaken an argument. Answering it well makes the argument stronger, because it shows the author has considered the other side.

example.prompt: “(1) The library should open on Sunday afternoons. (2) Many students work on Saturdays and have no quiet place to study. (3) When the library tested Sunday hours last spring, an average of 210 people came each Sunday. (4) Some say the library cannot afford more hours. (5) However, the library director reports that a literacy grant already covers the cost.”
steps: Sentence 1 says what should happen: claim. Sentence 2 says why: reason.
Sentence 3 gives a measured result: evidence.
“Some say” marks sentence 4 as the counterclaim. “However” marks sentence 5 as the rebuttal.

check.prompt:
Read the paragraph. Drag each sentence into the part of the argument it is.

“The city should plant trees along Harbor Avenue. A city survey found that Harbor Avenue's sidewalks reach 125 degrees on summer afternoons. Some residents argue that tree roots will crack the sidewalks. But the city forester says new root barriers prevent that damage.”
check.hint: Look for signal words: should, a survey found, some argue, but.
check.explain: The first sentence says what should happen (claim). The survey sentence gives a measured fact (evidence). “Some residents argue” states the other side (counterclaim). “But the city forester says…” answers that worry (rebuttal).
choices: The city should plant trees along Harbor Avenue.
A city survey found that Harbor Avenue's sidewalks reach 125 degrees on summer afternoons.
Some residents argue that tree roots will crack the sidewalks.
But the city forester says new root barriers prevent that damage.
check.why: The most common mistake is calling the forester's statement evidence because it quotes an expert. It does contain evidence, but its job here is to answer the residents' worry, so it is the rebuttal.

screens.title: Kinds of evidence
screens.html:
Evidence is the proof behind a reason. Learn to name the common kinds:

KindExample
StatisticsFines brought in $21,500 last year.
Research studyA study of 9,000 students in eight districts found…
Expert statementThe city forester says root barriers work.
Comparable caseWhen Oakdale added a Sunday market, attendance held steady.
AnecdoteA personal story: “Last spring, I watched a mother…”
Observation“On summer weekends, the lawn is full of families.”

Anecdotes and observations make an argument vivid, but they cover few cases. Statistics and research from a named source usually cover many.

check.prompt:
“Residents want a dog park. When Fairfield opened a fenced dog park in 2022, its parks department counted about 400 visitors a week within the first year.”

What kind of evidence does the second sentence give?
check.hint: Is the sentence about this town or a different one? Is it a story, an opinion, or a count?
check.explain: The sentence describes what happened in a different town (Fairfield) after it did what the writer proposes, with a visitor count from the parks department. That is a comparable case with statistics. The survey choice is tempting because it involves numbers, but no one was asked a question.
options: A comparable case from another town, with a count of visitors
A personal story about one resident and her dog
An expert's opinion about what dogs need
A survey asking residents of this town what kind of dog park they want
why: There is no story about one person here. The sentence reports what happened in another town, with a number.
No expert gives an opinion. The parks department counted visitors, which is a measured result, not a view about what dogs need.
The sentence is about Fairfield, not this town, and it counts visitors. Nobody was asked what they want.

screens.title: Test 1: Is the evidence relevant?
screens.html:
Test every piece of evidence three ways. The first test is relevance: is the evidence actually about this claim?

A fact can be true, specific, and from a great source and still be irrelevant. If the claim is about traffic danger at one intersection, the history of the street's paving is not relevant. Neither is crash data from a different city, unless the author shows the two places are alike.

Irrelevant evidence often sits right next to the topic. Ask: “If this is true, does it make the claim more likely?” If the answer is no, it is not relevant.

check.prompt: The writer claims the town should build a covered bus shelter at the Central Street stop. Click the sentence that is not relevant to that claim.
check.hint: For each sentence, ask: if this is true, does it help decide whether to build the shelter?
check.explain: The number of riders, the long waits, and the cost all bear on whether a shelter should be built. The history of the street's name tells us nothing about riders' needs, so it is not relevant. Relevant does not mean “supports the writer”; it means “about this claim.”
spans: The Central Street stop serves about 600 riders a day, more than any other stop in town.
Riders there now wait in the open, and the transit agency's records show average waits of 18 minutes.
Central Street was named for the town's first central school, which opened in 1904.
A shelter of the size needed would cost about $9,000, according to the transit agency.
check.why: The most common mistake is clicking the cost sentence because it seems like a reason against the shelter. Cost is relevant: it is information a reader needs to judge whether to build the shelter. The street's name history is not.

screens.title: Tests 2 and 3: Sufficient and reliable
screens.html:
Sufficient means there is enough evidence to cover the size of the claim. One story, or a handful of cases, cannot prove what is true for a whole town or a whole group.

Reliable means the evidence comes from a trustworthy source and was gathered fairly. Ask: Who collected it? How? Could I check it? An online poll that anyone can answer is not reliable for a whole town, because the people who answer choose themselves and may not represent everyone.

example.prompt: Claim: “Residents clearly want the town to go fine-free.” Evidence: “In an online poll on a neighborhood message board, 80 percent of the 150 people who responded agreed.”
steps: The claim is about residents, the whole town.
The poll counted only 150 people who chose to answer on one message board. That is not sufficient for a whole town.
People who answer online polls choose themselves, so they may not represent the town. That makes it less reliable.
example.answer: The 80 percent sounds strong, but the poll is too small and self-selected to prove what the whole town wants.

check.prompt:
Claim: “Teenagers in our county are spending too much time on their phones.” Evidence: “My two nephews are on their phones from the moment they wake up.”

The evidence is relevant. Which of the other two tests does it fail most clearly? Type one word: sufficient or reliable.
check.hint: Compare the size of the claim (a whole county) with the size of the evidence.
check.explain: The claim covers every teenager in the county, but the evidence is two people. Two cases are not enough to cover a claim that size, so the evidence is not sufficient. (It is also a casual observation, but the clearest failure is the tiny number of cases.)

mistakes.why: Reliability is about whether the source is trustworthy and fair. The bigger problem here is size: two nephews cannot speak for every teenager in a county. That is the sufficiency test.
The question says the evidence is relevant; it is about teenagers and phones. Choose between the other two tests: is the problem the source, or the amount?

screens.title: Reasoning and hidden assumptions
screens.html:
Reasoning is the bridge between the evidence and the claim. Part of that bridge is often unstated. An assumption is an idea the author takes for granted and needs you to accept.

To find it, ask: What must be true for this evidence to prove this claim?

A very common assumption is that one place, group, or time is like another: “It worked there, so it will work here.” If the two places are very different, the bridge is shaky and the argument is weaker.

example.prompt: “A nearby town added a Sunday farmers market and now draws 1,500 shoppers each week, so our town should add one too.”
steps: Evidence: the nearby town's Sunday market draws 1,500 shoppers.
Claim: our town should add a Sunday market.
What must be true? Our town must be similar enough (size, interest, vendors) that a Sunday market would succeed here too.
example.answer: Assumption: our town is similar enough to the nearby town for the same result to happen here.

check.prompt:
“The Eastside gym started offering free childcare during morning classes, and its morning attendance rose 30 percent. Our community center should offer free childcare during its morning classes too.”

Which assumption does this argument depend on?
check.hint: The evidence comes from another place. What must be true about our community center for that evidence to count?
check.explain: The evidence is about Eastside; the claim is about our center. For the evidence to matter, our center's members must respond the same way: free childcare must bring more of them to morning classes. If our members do not have young children, the argument falls apart. The cost choice is tempting, but the writer argues from attendance, not from profit.
options: Parents who use our community center would come to morning classes more if childcare were free.
The Eastside gym charges higher membership fees than our community center charges.
Morning classes are more popular than evening classes at most gyms and community centers in the area.
Free childcare costs a gym less than it earns from the extra members it attracts.
why: Fees are not part of the argument. The writer never compares prices, and the conclusion would not need this to be true.
The argument is about whether childcare raises attendance, not whether mornings beat evenings. This could be false and the argument would still hold.
The writer argues that childcare would raise attendance, not that it would make money. Cost is a different question the writer does not raise.

screens.title: Faulty reasoning: too little proof
screens.html:
Faulty reasoning (also called a logical fallacy) is a flaw in logic that makes an argument seem stronger than it is. Two common flaws stretch too little proof too far.

FlawWhat it doesExample
Hasty generalizationDraws a big conclusion from too few cases“I saw two drivers run that light, so everyone on this street drives recklessly.”
False causeAssumes that because B came after A, A caused B“Crime went up the year the mall opened, so the mall caused it.”

For a hasty generalization, ask: “Is this enough cases to cover everyone?” For false cause, ask: “What else could explain it?”

check.prompt:
Name the flaw in each statement.

“Our town started allowing scooter rentals in April, and in May the number of injuries reported downtown went up. The scooters must be causing those injuries.” {{0}}

“The two waiters I met at that restaurant were rude, so the whole staff must be rude.” {{1}}
check.hint: Is the writer relying on timing (this happened after that) or on too few examples?
check.explain:
Scooters: the rise in injuries came after the rentals began, but the writer never shows that a scooter was involved in any of them. Warmer weather or more people downtown could explain it. That is false cause.

Waiters: two people cannot represent an entire staff. That is a hasty generalization.

options: false cause
hasty generalization
either-or
bandwagon
why: The writer is not judging a whole group from a few examples. The problem is the link: the writer never shows that any of the injuries involved scooters, so timing alone is treated as proof of cause.
Either-or offers only two choices. This statement offers no choices; it blames scooters because the injuries came after them.
Bandwagon says something is right because many people believe it. Nobody's opinion is counted here.

options: false cause
hasty generalization
slippery slope
attack on the person
why: False cause is about one event following another. Here nothing happens after anything; the writer judges a whole staff from two people.
A slippery slope predicts a chain of worse results. This statement makes no prediction; it stretches two cases to cover everyone.
Attack on the person dismisses someone's argument by criticizing them. Here no argument is being answered; the problem is the size of the sample.

screens.title: Faulty reasoning: false choices and chains
screens.html:
Two more flaws trap readers by limiting how they think about the future.

FlawWhat it doesExample
Slippery slopeClaims one step will lead to a chain of worse and worse results, without proving each step“If we allow food trucks this summer, soon downtown will be nothing but food trucks.”
Either-or (false dilemma)Offers only two choices when more exist“Either we build a new school or our kids get no education.”

Slippery-slope sentences often use then, next, soon, before long. Either-or sentences often use either… or or the only choice. Ask: “Is each step proven?” and “Are these really the only options?”

check.prompt:
“The choice is simple: either we close the Westside pool, or we raise every resident's water bill. There is no other way to balance the parks budget.”

What is the main problem with this reasoning?
check.hint: Count the choices the writer offers. Are there really only that many?
check.explain: “Either… or” and “There is no other way” offer only two choices. A parks budget can be balanced in many ways, so this is an either-or (false dilemma). The slippery-slope choice is tempting because the argument is about something bad happening, but no chain of events is predicted.
options: It ignores other options, such as grants, sponsors, or cuts elsewhere in the parks budget.
It predicts that closing one pool will lead, step by step, to closing every pool and park in the city.
It concludes that all pools lose money based on the cost of one pool.
It criticizes the people who use the Westside pool instead of their reasons.
why: That would be a slippery slope, a chain of worse results. The writer predicts no chain; the writer offers only two choices.
That would be a hasty generalization. The writer does not judge all pools; the problem is that only two options are offered.
That would be an attack on the person. The writer never mentions or criticizes the pool's users.

screens.title: Faulty reasoning: attacking or twisting the other side
screens.html:
Some flaws avoid the other side's reasons instead of answering them.

FlawWhat it doesExample
Attack on the personCriticizes the people on the other side instead of their reasons“Don't listen to his plan for the parks. He doesn't even own a house here.”
Straw manTwists the other side's view into a weaker version that is easy to knock down“My opponents want to get rid of all rules.” (when they asked to change one)

Ask: “Did the author answer the argument, or the arguer?” and “Is that what the other side actually said?”

check.prompt: A council member wrote this about a proposal to let food trucks park on Main Street two evenings a week. Click the sentence that is a straw man.
check.hint: Compare what the proposal actually says with how one sentence describes the supporters.
check.explain: The proposal is limited (four trucks, two evenings) and has rules (permits and inspections). Saying supporters want “anyone with a truck and no rules at all” twists their position into something much weaker and easier to attack. That is a straw man. The other sentences describe the proposal accurately or state the writer's position.
spans: The food truck proposal would allow up to four trucks on Main Street on Thursday and Friday evenings.
Supporters of the plan want to hand our downtown over to anyone with a truck and no rules at all.
Each truck would need a city permit and a health inspection, just as restaurants do.
I believe the council should wait for the parking study before voting.
check.why: Students sometimes click the sentence about waiting for the parking study because it opposes the plan. Opposing a plan is not a flaw; the straw man is the sentence that twists a limited, rule-bound proposal into “no rules at all.”

screens.title: Faulty reasoning: crowds and feelings
screens.html:
FlawWhat it doesExample
BandwagonSays something is right because many people believe it or do it“Everyone is switching to this plan, so it must be right.”
Appeal to emotion / loaded languageUses fear, pity, anger, or charged words in place of evidence“Only a heartless council would let our beloved park be destroyed.”

Emotion is not always a flaw. A moving story next to solid data is fine. It becomes a flaw when the feeling is doing the work the evidence should do. Test it: remove the emotional words. What proof is left?

check.prompt: Which two sentences use popularity or emotion in place of evidence? Select two answers.
check.hint: For each sentence, remove the feelings and the crowd. Is there any proof left?
check.explain: The phone-plan sentence treats the number of sign-ups as proof that the plan is a good deal: bandwagon. The bus sentence uses guilt and loaded words (“truly loves,” “a driver like that”) with no facts about the driver: appeal to emotion. The other three give prices, inspection results, and survey data.
options: Thousands of people have already signed up for the new phone plan, so it must be the best deal.
Any parent who truly loves their children would never let them ride a bus with a driver like that.
The plan costs $35 a month, which is $10 less than the company's previous lowest price.
A state inspection found that 3 of the district's 40 buses had faulty brake lights.
The parents' group surveyed all 212 bus riders' families, and 61 percent reported late pickups.
why: This is a specific, checkable price comparison. It is evidence, not popularity or emotion.
This is a finding from a state inspection with exact numbers. It is evidence, not an emotional appeal.
This is a survey of every rider's family, with a stated result. It is evidence, not an appeal to feelings.

screens.title: Judging a source: Who, What, When, Why
screens.html:
Evidence is only as good as its source. Ask four questions:

  • Who wrote it? Does the person or group have real knowledge of the subject?
  • What evidence does it give? Data and methods you could check, or just opinions?
  • When was it written? Is it current for your question?
  • Why was it written? Does the author gain money, votes, or customers if you agree?

A source with something to gain is not automatically wrong. It means you should look harder at its evidence. A source with data, clear methods, and no stake in the outcome usually deserves the most trust.

check.prompt: A reader wants to know whether a new medicine is safe. Which source is most credible?
check.hint: Run Who, What, When, Why on each source. Which one passes all four?
check.explain: Apply the four questions. The university study: independent researchers (Who), 2,000 tracked patients (What), recent (When), no sales stake (Why). The forum is tempting because 300 people sounds like many, but the posts are self-selected and unchecked.
options: A 2024 study by independent university researchers who tracked 2,000 patients taking the medicine
A 2024 television ad from the company that makes the medicine, featuring satisfied patients
A 2016 article written before the medicine was approved, quoting a doctor's predictions
A popular online forum where more than 300 users describe their own experiences with the medicine in detail
why: The company profits from sales (Why), and an ad is designed to sell, not to test safety. Satisfied patients are anecdotes.
This was written before anyone took the approved medicine (When), and a prediction is not a result.
Forum users chose to post, so they may not represent typical patients, and their reports are not checked. That is less reliable than a tracked study.

screens.title: Credible is not the same as relevant
screens.html:
A source can be trustworthy and still not answer your question. Always check both:

  1. Is it credible? (Who, What, When, Why)
  2. Is it about my exact question? (same place, same time, same thing)

A careful national study of bike lanes is credible, but if it did not include your city's street, it can only suggest what might have happened there. A prediction made before a change is not evidence of what happened after it.

example.prompt: Question: “Did the protected bike lane on Elm Street make Elm Street safer?” Source: a peer-reviewed study of protected lanes in 12 other cities, which found crashes fell 30 percent on average.
steps: Credible? Yes: university researchers, peer-reviewed, data from 12 cities.
About Elm Street? No: Elm Street's city was not one of the 12.
So it is credible but only indirectly relevant. It suggests a likely result; it does not show what happened on Elm Street.
example.answer: Credible, but not direct evidence for this question.

check.prompt:
Question: “Did the after-school tutoring program at Westside Middle School raise students' math scores?”

A 2023 national study of tutoring at 50 other schools is {{0}}. A 2019 newspaper quote in which the principal predicted the program would raise scores is {{1}}.
check.hint: For each source, ask two questions: Is it trustworthy? Is it about what actually happened at Westside?
check.explain: The national study is careful research, but Westside was not studied, so it is credible yet only indirect evidence. The principal's quote is from before the program produced results; a prediction is not evidence of an outcome. The best evidence would be Westside's own math scores before and after the program.

options: credible but not direct evidence about Westside
not credible because it is a national study
the best evidence because it is the largest
why: Being national does not make a study less credible. The problem is that Westside was not one of the schools studied.
Size makes a study credible, but this one did not include Westside, so it cannot show what happened there.

options: strong evidence because a principal is an expert
weak evidence because it is a prediction, not a result
weak evidence because newspapers are never credible
why: Expertise does not turn a prediction into a result. The quote came before the program had any results to report.
Newspapers can be credible sources. The problem is what the quote contains: a prediction made before the program ran.

screens.title: What strengthens or weakens an argument
screens.html:
The GED often asks, “Which statement, if true, would most weaken (or strengthen) the argument?” Treat each choice as true and ask what it does to the argument.

  1. Find the claim.
  2. Find the key evidence.
  3. Name the assumption that links them.
  4. A choice that supports the assumption strengthens. A choice that breaks it, often by giving another cause or showing the places are different, weakens.

Choices that repeat evidence already in the passage, or that are about a side issue, change nothing.

example.prompt: “The school should keep the new reading software, because reading scores rose 8 percent the year it was introduced.” Which weakens it: (a) the same year, the school also hired five reading tutors; (b) the software was installed in September?
steps: Claim: keep the software. Evidence: scores rose the year it was introduced.
Assumption: the software caused the rise.
(a) gives another possible cause, so it weakens the argument. (b) is a timing detail that changes nothing.
example.answer: (a) weakens the argument by offering another explanation for the higher scores.

check.prompt:
“Our city should paint bright bike lanes on Oak Avenue. After Millbrook painted bright bike lanes on its main street, bicycle crashes there fell by half within two years.”

Which statement, if true, would most strengthen the argument?
check.hint: Name the assumption first. Which fact makes it more likely to be true?
check.explain: The argument assumes Oak Avenue is like Millbrook's main street, so the same lanes would bring the same drop in crashes. Showing that the two streets have similar traffic, speeds, and cyclists supports that assumption and strengthens the argument. The attractiveness choice is tempting because it praises the lanes, but looks are not safety.
options: Oak Avenue and Millbrook's main street carry similar traffic, speeds, and numbers of cyclists.
Millbrook's lanes were painted green, which many residents said looked attractive.
Bicycle riding has become more popular in many cities across the country over the last ten years.
Our city painted new crosswalks on Oak Avenue three years ago.
why: How the lanes looked to residents does not show that the same safety result would happen on Oak Avenue.
This is a general trend in many cities. It does not connect Millbrook's result to Oak Avenue, and more riders could even mean more crashes.
Crosswalks are a different project. This fact says nothing about whether bike lanes would cut crashes on Oak Avenue.

screens.title: Putting it together: how the GED asks
screens.html:
On the GED, argument questions use wording like this:

  • “Which statement best expresses the author's claim?”
  • “Which evidence best supports the claim that…?”
  • “Which claim in the passage is not supported by evidence?”
  • “How does the author respond to the counterclaim in paragraph 3?”
  • “Which statement, if true, would most weaken the argument?”

To find an unsupported claim, look for statements with no source, no number, and no example, especially ones with everyone, clearly, always, or obviously. Those words often signal that the writer is asking you to accept something without proof.

check.prompt:
(1) The county should extend the Route 9 bus to the new hospital. (2) The transit agency counted 340 riders a day transferring to taxis at the end of Route 9 last month. (3) The hospital reports that 22 percent of missed appointments involve patients who list “no ride” as the reason. (4) Clearly, everyone in the county supports this change. (5) The agency estimates the extension would cost $210,000 a year.

Which sentence makes a claim that is not supported by evidence?
check.hint: Look for a sentence with no source and no number, especially one using a word like everyone or clearly.
check.explain: The sentence beginning “Clearly, everyone” gives no survey, number, or source, and “everyone” is far broader than any evidence in the paragraph. It is an unsupported, bandwagon-style claim. The cost sentence is tempting because it does not help the writer's case, but it is still backed by a named source.
options: “Clearly, everyone in the county supports this change.”
“The transit agency counted 340 riders a day transferring to taxis at the end of Route 9 last month.”
“The hospital reports that 22 percent of missed appointments involve patients who list ‘no ride’ as the reason.”
“The agency estimates the extension would cost $210,000 a year.”
why: This is supported: it is a count by the transit agency, a named source, of a specific number of riders.
This is supported: the hospital's own records give a specific percent and reason.
This is supported: a named agency gives a specific estimate. It is not a reason for the claim, but it is not unsupported.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:

  • An argument has a claim (what the author wants), reasons, and evidence. Strong arguments answer a counterclaim with a rebuttal.
  • Test evidence three ways: relevant (about this claim?), sufficient (enough?), reliable (trustworthy and fairly gathered?).
  • Find the assumption: what must be true for this evidence to prove this claim?
  • Watch for faulty reasoning: hasty generalization, false cause, slippery slope, either-or, attack on the person, bandwagon, straw man, appeal to emotion.
  • Judge sources with Who, What, When, Why. Credible is not the same as relevant.
  • To weaken an argument, break its assumption; to strengthen it, support the assumption.
  • On test day: cover your opinion, check the proof.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: Fines Don't Bring the Books Back
stimuli.html:
An opinion column by Dana Whitfield, a retired school librarian who volunteers with the Friends of the Brookdale Library

(1) Today, 1,240 Brookdale residents cannot borrow a single book from their public library. Their cards are blocked because each of them owes more than $10 in late fines. That is about one of every nine active library cards in town. Next month, the library board will vote on whether to stop charging fines for overdue materials. The board should vote yes. Late fines do little to get books returned, they raise very little money, and they push away the very people a public library is meant to serve.

(2) Supporters of fines argue that the charges teach responsibility and give borrowers a reason to return items on time. It is a fair concern, but the evidence does not back it up. When the Lakeview County Library stopped charging late fines in 2021, it tracked what happened next. Before the change, 92 percent of borrowed items came back within one week of their due date. Two years after the change, the figure was 91 percent, nearly the same. Under the Brookdale plan, anyone who keeps an item more than a month past its due date would still be billed for it, so people would still have every reason to bring books back.

(3) Some board members worry that the library cannot afford to give up the money. The numbers say otherwise. Last year, fines brought in $21,500, less than 1 percent of the library's $2.6 million budget. Collecting that money is not free, either. Library director Marisol Grant estimates that staff members spend about 600 hours a year collecting fines, processing payments, and settling disputes over charges. At the library's average staff wage of $22 an hour, that time costs about $13,200. Once that cost is subtracted, fines bring in only about $8,300 a year, and those 600 hours could be spent helping patrons instead.

(4) The real cost of fines falls on the people who can least afford them. According to the library's own records, more than half of the blocked cards belong to children and teenagers, who often have no way to pay a fine themselves. Last spring, I stood behind a mother at the checkout desk who had to put back the picture books her six-year-old son had chosen because she could not pay a $14 balance. When Lakeview dropped its fines, more than 3,100 residents whose cards had been blocked came back and began borrowing again within the first year.

(5) Residents clearly want this change. In an online poll on a neighborhood message board last month, 80 percent of the 150 people who responded said the library should go fine-free.

(6) The evidence shows that it would reopen the library to more than a thousand residents while costing the library very little. A library's job is to put books into people's hands, not to keep them out. The board should vote yes.

stimuli.title: Letter to the Editor: Keep the East Lawn Open
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

(1) On March 12, the town council will vote on a plan to build a skate park on the east lawn of Fairview Park. I have lived on Linden Street, across from the park, for thirty-one years, and I urge the council to vote no.

(2) First, consider the cost. According to the parks department's own estimate, the skate park would cost $310,000 to build and about $12,000 a year to maintain. That is a significant amount of money for a town of our size, and the council has not explained where it would come from.

(3) Second, a skate park would bring trouble. Last Saturday, I watched two teenagers on skateboards toss soda cans into the bushes by the playground. If that is how skaters treat the park now, imagine how they will treat a park built just for them. Look at what happened in Cedar Hills. That town opened a skate park in 2019, and the next year car break-ins there went up. Clearly, the skate park caused it.

(4) Third, the skate park would take space that many people already use. On summer weekends, the east lawn is full of families having picnics and children playing pickup soccer. If we approve a skate park this year, next year skaters will demand lights, then a snack stand, then a parking lot, and before long the whole park will be paved over. The council should protect the lawn for the many residents who enjoy it now.

(5) Fourth, the people pushing this project hardly represent the town. Most of them moved here in the last few years and do not understand what Fairview Park means to the families who have been here for generations. Meanwhile, everyone I have talked to on my street is against the plan.

(6) Finally, the council needs to set priorities. The choice is simple: either we spend $310,000 on a skate park, or we fix the potholes on Main Street. We cannot do both.

(7) Fairview Park belongs to all of us. I ask the council to keep it that way and vote no.

Gordon Pell
Linden Street

stimuli.title: Draft Letter: We Need a Safe Crossing on Oak Street
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

(1) The town should install a marked crosswalk with a flashing pedestrian signal where Oak Street meets Fifth Avenue. Every day, hundreds of people cross Oak Street at this corner to reach the senior center, the Route 4 bus stop, and Grover's Market. Right now, they have no crosswalk, no signal, and no stop sign to slow drivers down.

(2) This crossing is dangerous. (A) Two of those crashes sent pedestrians to the hospital. Most of the people who were hurt were walking to or from the senior center.

(3) Some residents argue that a signal would slow traffic on one of the town's busiest streets. (B) the town's traffic engineer estimates that the signal would add less than 30 seconds to the average drive along Oak Street. That is a small price for a safer crossing.

(4) Cost is not a barrier, either. A similar signal installed at Maple Street last year cost about $45,000, and the town already has money set aside in (C) road safety fund for exactly this kind of project.

(5) (D) I urge the council to act before anyone else is hurt.

Lena Ortiz
Fifth Avenue

stimuli.title: Sources on the Elm Street Bike Lane
stimuli.html:
A student is researching this question: Did the protected bike lane that opened on Elm Street in Riverton in 2021 make Elm Street safer? The student found these five sources.

SourceAuthor and dateWhat it says
ARiverton Department of Transportation, “Elm Street Safety Review,” 2025Compares police crash reports on Elm Street for the three years before the lane opened (2018–2020) and the three years after (2022–2024). Total crashes fell from 47 to 29; crashes involving cyclists fell from 11 to 6. Full data tables and methods are included.
BBlog post by the owner of a bicycle shop on Elm Street, 2024“The new lane has made Elm Street the safest street in the city. Business has never been better!” No data are given.
CArticle in a peer-reviewed transportation research journal by university researchers, 2023Studied protected bike lanes in 12 cities and found that crashes fell by an average of 30 percent on streets after protected lanes were added. Riverton was not one of the 12 cities.
DComment by a resident in a neighborhood social media group, 2025“I nearly got hit by a cyclist on Elm last week. These lanes are a disaster.”

stimuli.title: Open the Doors: Make the Rec Center Free for Teens
stimuli.html:
An opinion column by Marcus Bell, a volunteer basketball coach at the Ridgeway Recreation Center

(1) Every weekday afternoon, the Ridgeway Recreation Center offers open gym, a homework room, and a computer lab. Teens pay $5 a visit to use them. That fee sounds small, but it adds up to about $100 a month for a teen who comes every school day. Next month, the city council will vote on a proposal to drop the fee for residents ages 13 to 18. The council should approve it. Free entry would bring more teens through the doors, it would cost the city little, and it would give young people a safe place to spend the hours after school.

(2) Some council members argue that teens will not respect a place they do not pay for and that damage to the building will rise. That worry is understandable, but the record of a nearby city does not support it. When the Millbrook Community Center ended its teen fee in 2022, its staff kept a log of damage reports. In the two years before the change, they recorded 14 reports of damaged equipment or property. In the two years after, they recorded 13. Meanwhile, average daily teen visits rose from 45 to 120.

(3) The cost to the city would be small. According to the parks department's budget report, teen fees brought in $18,400 last year, about 1 percent of the center's $1.9 million budget. Much of that money never reaches programs, either. The center pays a part-time front-desk cashier about $11,000 a year, mostly to collect teen fees. Without the fee, that position would no longer be needed.

(4) Most important, the hours after school matter. The county sheriff's office reports that more than a third of juvenile arrests in the county happen between 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. on school days. Last winter, a ninth grader I coach told me he had stopped coming because his mother had lost hours at work and he would not ask her for the money. He spent those afternoons alone in an empty apartment instead.

(5) The public is behind this idea. At our youth league's championship tournament in March, 300 people signed a petition asking the council to make the center free for teens.

(6) A free teen pass will not solve every problem young people face. But the numbers show it would bring more teens in while costing the city very little. The council should vote yes.

stimuli.title: Letter to the Editor: Keep Food Trucks Out of Riverside Square
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

(1) On April 8, the city council will vote on a plan to allow up to six food trucks to park on Riverside Square on Friday and Saturday evenings. I have owned Lund's Diner on the square for nineteen years, and I urge the council to vote no.

(2) First, the square does not have the room. The city's own parking study counted 84 spaces around the square and found that on Friday evenings, an average of 79 are already filled. Six food trucks would take at least twelve of those spaces. The fire marshal has also ruled that no vendor may park in the two fire lanes on the north side of the square, which leaves even less room.

(3) Second, food trucks bring trouble. Last month at the county fair, I saw one truck leave a pile of greasy boxes behind its stand. If that is how food truck owners treat a fairground, imagine what they will do to our square. And look at Brentwood. That city began allowing food trucks downtown in 2021, and the next year two of its restaurants closed. The food trucks obviously drove them out of business.

(4) Third, this plan is only the beginning. If we allow six trucks on weekends this year, next year there will be twenty trucks every night, then carnival rides, and before long the square will be nothing but a lot for traveling vendors.

(5) Fourth, the people behind this plan do not have the town's interests at heart. Most of them are out-of-town operators who have never paid a dollar of property tax here. And every customer I have spoken to at my diner agrees that the trucks are a bad idea.

(6) The council faces a clear choice: either it protects the restaurants that have served this town for decades, or it watches downtown die.

(7) Riverside Square is the heart of our town. I ask the council to keep it that way and vote no.

Teresa Lund
Owner, Lund's Diner

stimuli.title: Draft Letter: Light the Riverwalk
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

(1) The city should install lights along the half-mile Riverwalk path between Bridge Street and Mill Park. Hundreds of people use the path every evening to walk home from the train station, to exercise, or to reach night classes at Harbor Community College. After sunset, most of the path is completely dark.

(2) The darkness puts people at risk. (A) Seven of those incidents happened between October and February, when it gets dark before 6 p.m.

(3) Some residents worry that lights would disturb birds and other wildlife along the river. (B) a study by the state wildlife agency found that shielded, downward-facing lights had little (C) on birds nesting along rivers.

(4) The project is also affordable. The city's engineering office estimates that the lights would cost $160,000, and the state's Safe Routes program pays up to 80 percent of the cost of projects like this one.

(5) (D) Please light the Riverwalk before another winter comes.

Andre Whitaker
Mill Street
