items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the author's claim in the op-ed?
items.hint: Look for what the author wants the board to do. She states it in paragraph 1 and repeats it at the end.
items.explain:
Step 1. A claim is what the author wants readers to believe or do. Check paragraph 1 and the conclusion: “The board should vote yes” on whether to stop charging fines for overdue materials. She repeats this in paragraph 6.

Step 2. “The library board should vote to stop charging late fines” matches. Correct.

Step 3. Check the traps. The one-in-nine figure is evidence the author uses, not her claim. “Fines teach responsibility” is the counterclaim she argues against in paragraph 2. Cutting staff hours is never suggested; in fact, she says the 600 hours could go to helping patrons.
options: The library board should vote to stop charging late fines on overdue materials.
About one of every nine active library cards in Brookdale is currently blocked.
Late fines teach borrowers to be responsible and return items on time.
The library should cut staff hours to make up for the money it loses from fines.
why: This is a statistic from paragraph 1. It is evidence the author uses to show how many people fines shut out, not what she wants the board to do.
This is the counterclaim from paragraph 2, the view of fine supporters that the author argues against.
The author never suggests cutting staff hours. She says the 600 hours spent on fines could go to helping patrons instead.

items.prompt: What kind of evidence does the author use in paragraph 2 to respond to people who say fines get books returned on time?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 2 and look at the numbers. Where do they come from, and what do they compare?
items.explain:
Step 1. Paragraph 2 reports that at the Lakeview County Library, 92 percent of items came back within a week before fines ended and 91 percent two years after.

Step 2. These are statistics comparing return rates before and after a change at another library. Correct.

Step 3. The personal story about the mother and son is in paragraph 4, and the online poll is in paragraph 5, so they are not used in paragraph 2. No expert on library budgets is quoted anywhere; the director's estimate in paragraph 3 is about staff hours.
options: Statistics comparing return rates at another library before and after it ended fines
A personal story about a family at the library checkout desk
A quotation from an expert who studies library budgets and the effects of fines on borrowers
The results of an online poll of local residents
why: The story of the mother and her son is in paragraph 4, where it shows who is hurt by fines. Paragraph 2 uses numbers from another library.
No one who studies library budgets is quoted. The director's estimate in paragraph 3 is about staff hours, and it is not in paragraph 2.
The online poll is in paragraph 5 and is about what residents want. Paragraph 2 compares return rates at another library.

items.prompt: The author claims that ending late fines would cost the library very little. Which two details best support this part of her argument? Select two answers.
items.hint: The question is about money. Which details mention dollars the library would lose or save?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the part of the argument: ending fines would cost the library very little. Relevant evidence must be about money.

Step 2. Fines are less than 1 percent of the budget (paragraph 3): the lost income is small. Correct. Collecting fines takes about 600 staff hours worth about $13,200, so the library keeps only about $8,300 ($21,500 − $13,200 = $8,300). Correct.

Step 3. The other details are real evidence from the op-ed, but they support different points: who is hurt by fines (children and teenagers, blocked cards), whether books still come back (Lakeview return rates), or public opinion (the poll). None of them is about cost.
options: Fines brought in $21,500 last year, which is less than 1 percent of the library's $2.6 million budget.
Staff spend about 600 hours a year handling fines, time worth about $13,200 in wages.
More than half of the blocked cards belong to children and teenagers.
At Lakeview, 92 percent of items were returned within a week before fines ended, and 91 percent after.
Eighty percent of 150 people who answered an online poll said the library should go fine-free.
About 1,240 residents currently have blocked library cards.
why: This is real evidence, but it supports a different point: who is hurt by fines. It says nothing about money.
This supports the point that books still come back without fines. It is not about what fines cost or earn.
This is about public opinion, not cost. (It is also weak evidence, as you will see.)
This shows how many people fines shut out. It does not show that ending fines would be cheap.

items.prompt: How does the author respond to the counterclaim that fines teach responsibility and get items returned on time?
items.hint: Find the paragraph where the counterclaim appears. What does the author say right after it?
items.explain:
Step 1. The counterclaim appears at the start of paragraph 2: “Supporters of fines argue that the charges teach responsibility and give borrowers a reason to return items on time.”

Step 2. The next sentences are the rebuttal: “It is a fair concern, but the evidence does not back it up,” followed by Lakeview's return rates (92 percent before, 91 percent after). Correct.

Step 3. The author never mentions teaching responsibility at home. The children-and-teenagers detail is from paragraph 4 and supports a different point (who is hurt by fines). She never attacks supporters of fines personally; that would be faulty reasoning, and it is not in the text.
options: She calls it a fair concern, then shows that return rates at a library without fines stayed nearly the same.
She argues that responsibility should be taught at home rather than by the library.
She points out that more than half of the blocked cards belong to children and teenagers.
She suggests that people who support fines rarely use the library themselves.
why: The author never mentions teaching responsibility at home. Her answer to the counterclaim is evidence from Lakeview.
This detail is from paragraph 4 and supports a different point (who is hurt by fines). It does not answer whether fines get books returned.
The author never attacks fine supporters. She calls their view “a fair concern” and answers it with evidence; an attack on the person would be faulty reasoning.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author states that “residents clearly want this change.” Why does the evidence she gives provide weak support for this statement?
items.hint: Think about who answered the poll and how they were chosen.
items.explain:
Step 1. The claim is broad: residents clearly want the change. The proof is one online poll with 150 responses on a neighborhood message board.

Step 2. The people who answered chose themselves; they are people who use that message board and cared enough to respond. That small, self-selected group may not represent the town. The evidence is not sufficient or reliable for such a broad claim. Correct.

Step 3. Last month is recent, so timing is not the problem. Eighty percent is a large majority, not a small share. Asking about late fines is exactly the relevant question; the budget is a different issue.
options: The poll counted only 150 people who chose to answer on a message board, so they may not represent most residents.
The poll was taken last month, so its results are already out of date.
Eighty percent is too small a share to show that people support a change.
The poll asked residents about late fines instead of asking them about the library's overall budget and spending priorities.
why: Last month is recent, so timing is not the problem. The problem is who answered the poll.
Eighty percent is a large majority. If the poll were fair, 80 percent would be strong; the issue is that only 150 self-selected people answered.
Asking about late fines is exactly the right question for this claim. The budget is a different issue.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 of the letter is shown below. Click the sentence that claims, without evidence, that one decision will lead to a chain of worse and worse results.
items.hint: Look for a sentence that moves step by step from one event to bigger and bigger consequences.
items.explain:
Step 1. The prompt describes a slippery slope: one step is said to lead to a chain of increasingly bad results, with no proof for each step.

Step 2. “If we approve a skate park this year, next year skaters will demand lights, then a snack stand, then a parking lot, and before long the whole park will be paved over.” The writer offers no evidence that any of these later steps would happen. Correct.

Step 3. The first sentence is the paragraph's reason (topic sentence). The second is the writer's observation of how the lawn is used, which is relevant support. The last sentence restates what the writer wants the council to do.
spans: Third, the skate park would take space that many people already use.
On summer weekends, the east lawn is full of families having picnics and children playing pickup soccer.
If we approve a skate park this year, next year skaters will demand lights, then a snack stand, then a parking lot, and before long the whole park will be paved over.
The council should protect the lawn for the many residents who enjoy it now.
items.why: The most common mistake is clicking the topic sentence about taking space people already use. That sentence states a reason; the slippery slope is the sentence that jumps from one skate park to a fully paved park through a chain of unproven steps.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the letter criticizes the people who support the skate park instead of responding to their reasons?
items.hint: Look for a sentence about the supporters themselves, not about the skate park.
items.explain:
Step 1. An attack on the person (ad hominem) judges an idea by criticizing the people who hold it.

Step 2. In paragraph 5, the writer dismisses supporters because they are newcomers who supposedly “do not understand” the park. How long someone has lived in town says nothing about whether a skate park is a good idea. Correct.

Step 3. The other sentences are about the issue itself: the cost and funding of the project, how the lawn is used now, and what the writer wants the council to do. Whether or not you agree with them, none of them targets the supporters personally.
options: Most of them moved here in the last few years and do not understand what Fairview Park means to the families who have been here for generations.
That is a significant amount of money for a town of our size, and the council has not explained where it would come from.
On summer weekends, the east lawn is full of families having picnics and children playing pickup soccer.
The council should protect the lawn for the many residents who enjoy it now.
why: This sentence is about the project's cost and funding. It may be a fair point or not, but it is about the issue, not the supporters.
This describes how the lawn is used now. It is an observation about the park, not a criticism of the people on the other side.
This restates what the writer wants the council to do. It does not mention the supporters at all.

items.prompt:
Read the draft letter. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): This crossing is dangerous. {{0}} Two of those crashes sent pedestrians to the hospital.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): Some residents argue that a signal would slow traffic on one of the town's busiest streets. {{1}} the town's traffic engineer estimates that the signal would add less than 30 seconds to the average drive along Oak Street.

Paragraph 4, blank (C): The town already has money set aside in {{2}} road safety fund for exactly this kind of project.
items.hint: For (A), the next sentence says “Two of those crashes.” For (B), the sentence answers an objection. For (C), the word refers to “the town” and shows ownership.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The topic sentence claims the crossing is dangerous, so the next sentence should give relevant, reliable evidence. Step 2: The following sentence refers to “those crashes,” so the missing sentence must mention crashes. Step 3: “Police records show eleven crashes involving pedestrians at this intersection in the past three years” is relevant, specific, and from a checkable source. Correct. The paving history and the color of crosswalks are not about danger. The neighbor's comment is one person's opinion about drivers in general, not evidence about this intersection.

Blank (B). Step 1: The first sentence states a counterclaim (a signal would slow traffic). Step 2: The next sentence answers it with contrasting evidence, so a contrast transition is needed: “However,” Correct. “For example” would introduce an example of slowed traffic; “Similarly” signals agreement; “As a result” signals cause and effect. None fits a rebuttal.

Blank (C). Step 1: The word refers to “the town,” which is singular, and shows that the fund belongs to the town. Step 2: The singular possessive pronoun is its, with no apostrophe. Correct. “It's” means “it is” (“in it is road safety fund” makes no sense). “Their” is plural and does not agree with “town.” “Its'” is not a word.

options: Police records show eleven crashes involving pedestrians at this intersection in the past three years.
Oak Street was first paved in 1958 and has been repaved twice since then.
My neighbor says the drivers in this town are the worst she has ever seen.
Crosswalks in most towns are painted with white reflective stripes.
why: The paving history is not about danger, and the next sentence refers to “those crashes,” which this sentence never mentions.
This is one person's opinion about drivers in general. It is not evidence about this intersection and does not mention crashes.
This is a general fact about crosswalk paint. It is not about danger at Oak and Fifth and does not set up “those crashes.”

options: However,
For example,
Similarly,
As a result,
why: “For example” would introduce an example of slowed traffic. The sentence instead answers the worry with contrasting evidence.
“Similarly” signals agreement. The engineer's estimate pushes back against the worry, so a contrast word is needed.
“As a result” signals cause and effect. The engineer's estimate is not a result of the residents' worry; it answers it.

options: its
it's
their
its'
why: “It's” means “it is.” “In it is road safety fund” makes no sense. Ownership needs “its” with no apostrophe.
“Their” is plural, but it refers to “the town,” which is singular.
“Its'” is not a word in English. The possessive of “it” is “its.”

items.prompt: Which source gives the most credible and relevant evidence about whether the Elm Street lane itself made Elm Street safer?
items.hint: Use Who, What, When, Why, and remember that the question is about Elm Street specifically.
items.explain:
Step 1. The question is about one street: did this lane make Elm Street safer? The best source must be both credible and about Elm Street.

Step 2. Source A measures Elm Street crashes for three years before and three years after the lane, using police reports, and includes its data and methods so readers can check them (What). It is recent (When). Total crashes fell from 47 to 29. Correct. (A city reviewing its own project could have a stake in a good result, which is why its published data and methods matter.)

Step 3. Source C is credible research, but Riverton was not studied, so it is not direct evidence about Elm Street. Source B gives no data and the author has a business interest. Source D is one person's single experience.
options: Source A, the Riverton Department of Transportation's safety review
Source B, the blog post by the owner of a bicycle shop on Elm Street
Source C, the research article on protected bike lanes in 12 cities
Source D, the resident's comment in a social media group
why: The shop owner gives no data and has a business interest in the lane. A claim of “safest street in the city” with nothing to check is not reliable.
This is careful research, but Riverton was not one of the 12 cities. It is credible but does not measure what happened on Elm Street.
This is one person's single experience. It is not sufficient to show whether the street became safer overall.

items.prompt: Drag each statement from the letter into the category that best describes its reasoning.
items.hint: Ask of each statement: Is the conclusion based on too few cases? On timing alone? On only two choices? Or on relevant facts the writer could reasonably know?
items.explain:
Hasty generalization: The writer saw two teenagers litter once and concludes how all skaters will treat a skate park. Two people on one day are too few to judge a whole group.

False cause: Break-ins in Cedar Hills rose the year after its skate park opened, but timing alone does not prove the skate park caused them. The writer gives no evidence linking the two.

Either-or: The writer offers only two choices, a skate park or pothole repair, without showing that the town's budget allows only one. Other options (different funding sources, a smaller design, phasing the work) are ignored.

Reasonable support: The cost figures come from a named, official source (the parks department) and are relevant to whether the town should spend the money. The description of families using the lawn is an observation from someone who has lived across from the park for thirty-one years, and it is relevant to the claim that the park would take away space people use.
choices: Last Saturday, I watched two teenagers on skateboards toss soda cans into the bushes. If that is how skaters treat the park now, imagine how they will treat a park built just for them.
That town opened a skate park in 2019, and the next year car break-ins there went up. Clearly, the skate park caused it.
Either we spend $310,000 on a skate park, or we fix the potholes on Main Street. We cannot do both.
According to the parks department's own estimate, the skate park would cost $310,000 to build and about $12,000 a year to maintain.
On summer weekends, the east lawn is full of families having picnics and children playing pickup soccer.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the Cedar Hills break-in statement under hasty generalization. It does use only one town, but its main flaw is treating “the next year” as proof that the skate park caused the break-ins, which is false cause.

items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Sources C and E as evidence for the student's question?
items.hint: Check two things for each source: Is it trustworthy? Is it about what actually happened on Elm Street after 2021?
items.explain:
Step 1: Source C. It is peer-reviewed university research covering 12 cities, so it is credible. But Riverton was not one of the 12 cities, so it can only suggest what might happen on Elm Street. It is credible but only indirectly relevant.

Step 2: Source E. It was written in 2012, nine years before the lane opened, and it quotes a prediction. A prediction is not evidence of results.

Step 3. So neither source shows what actually happened on Elm Street. Correct.

Step 4. University researchers are not less credible than city officials. Being published before another source does not make research outdated, and an older prediction is less useful here, not more. Agreeing with each other is not the same as being biased; bias comes from a stake in the outcome or an unfair method.
options: Source C is careful research but does not include Elm Street, and Source E is a prediction made before the lane was built, so neither shows what actually happened on Elm Street.
Source C is not credible because it was written by university researchers instead of city officials, while Source E is credible because a city planner is an expert.
Source C is outdated because it was published before Source A, and Source E is the most reliable source because it was written first.
Both sources are biased because they agree that protected bike lanes reduce crashes.
why: University researchers are not less credible than city officials, and a planner's prediction from 2012 is not evidence of what happened after 2021.
Being published before another source does not make careful research outdated, and an older prediction is less useful here, not more.
Agreeing with each other is not the same as bias. Bias comes from a stake in the outcome or an unfair method, not from reaching the same conclusion.

items.prompt: Return to the library op-ed. Which statement, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?
items.hint: Which of the author's key pieces of evidence could a new fact undercut? Look especially at paragraph 2.
items.explain:
Step 1. A central reason in the op-ed is that ending fines does not hurt return rates. Her only evidence is one library, Lakeview, where return rates barely changed. Her reasoning assumes Brookdale would see the same result.

Step 2. If several similar libraries saw late returns rise sharply, that assumption falls apart, and the counterclaim (fines get books returned) gains support. Correct.

Step 3. The children-and-teenagers fact already appears in the op-ed and supports the author. E-books return themselves, so they say nothing about whether physical books come back without fines. A growing budget does not weaken the argument; if anything, it makes the small loss of fine income even less important.
options: At several libraries similar to Brookdale's, the share of items returned late rose sharply after late fines ended.
More than half of Brookdale's blocked library cards belong to children and teenagers.
Many libraries, including Brookdale's, now lend e-books that disappear from a reader's device automatically on the due date.
Brookdale's library budget has grown by about 2 percent a year over the last ten years.
why: This fact already appears in the op-ed, and it supports the author by showing who is hurt by fines. It cannot weaken her argument.
E-books return themselves on the due date, so they tell us nothing about whether physical books come back without fines.
A growing budget does not weaken the argument. If anything, it makes the small loss of fine income matter even less.

items.prompt:
Read the draft letter again. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 5, blank (D): The writer wants a closing sentence that restates the claim without faulty reasoning. {{0}} I urge the council to act before anyone else is hurt.

The writer's strongest evidence that the crossing is dangerous is {{1}}.
items.hint: For (D), read each choice and ask whether it gives a reason or attacks, predicts disaster, or follows the crowd. For the second blank, ask which detail actually measures danger.
items.explain:
Blank (D). A sound closing restates the claim and the main reasons. The sentence about protecting the hundreds of people who cross, at a cost already set aside, does that and draws on paragraphs 1 and 4. The other three choices are faulty reasoning: an attack on the person, a slippery slope, and a bandwagon appeal.

Second blank. The claim is that the crossing is dangerous, so the strongest evidence is a reliable record of harm at that spot: police records of pedestrian crashes, two of which sent people to the hospital. The list of nearby places is tempting because it shows heavy use, but heavy use alone does not prove danger.

options: A crosswalk and signal would protect the hundreds of people who cross here every day, at a cost the town has already set aside.
Any council member who votes against this crosswalk clearly does not care about the seniors in our town.
If the council waits, there will soon be crashes at every corner in town, and no one will dare walk anywhere.
Every town worth living in already has a signal at a corner as busy as this one.
why: This attacks the people who might vote no instead of answering their reasons. It is an attack on the person, the kind of faulty reasoning the writer wants to avoid.
This is a slippery slope: it jumps from one corner to crashes everywhere with no evidence for any step.
This is a bandwagon appeal with loaded language (“worth living in”). It gives no evidence, only a claim that other towns do it.

options: the police record of crashes involving pedestrians at the intersection
the estimate that a signal would add less than 30 seconds to drives
the cost of the similar signal installed at Maple Street last year
the list of places people walk to near the corner of Oak and Fifth
why: This answers the traffic counterclaim in paragraph 3. It says nothing about how dangerous the crossing is.
This supports the point that the signal is affordable. It does not show danger.
This shows why many people cross here, which matters, but it does not show that crossing is dangerous. Crash records do.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the op-ed.

The story in paragraph 4 about the mother and her son is {{0}}. The Lakeview evidence in paragraph 2 supports the author's claim only if the reader assumes that {{1}}.
items.hint: For the first blank, use the three evidence tests. For the second, ask what must be true for numbers from another library to prove something about Brookdale.
items.explain:
First blank. The story is relevant and makes the problem easy to picture, but it is one family. It is not sufficient to show how fines affect borrowers in general; the library's records (more than half of blocked cards belong to young people) do that job better.

Second blank. The Lakeview numbers come from another library. They prove something about Brookdale only if Brookdale borrowers would behave the same way after fines end. That is the unstated assumption. The budget choice is tempting because money is discussed elsewhere in the op-ed, but it has nothing to do with return rates.

options: vivid, but one family's experience cannot show how fines affect most borrowers
the strongest evidence in the op-ed, because the author saw it with her own eyes
irrelevant, because it is about a child rather than an adult borrower
the counterclaim, which the author answers in the next paragraph
why: Seeing something firsthand makes a story vivid, not sufficient. One case is weaker than the library's records about more than half of the blocked cards.
It is relevant: the author's claim is that fines push away people the library serves, and children are among them. Its weakness is size, not relevance.
The counterclaim is in paragraph 2 (fines teach responsibility). The story supports the author's own position.

options: Brookdale borrowers would respond to ending fines the way Lakeview borrowers did
Lakeview's library has a larger budget than the Brookdale library has
most overdue items at both libraries are children's picture books
the Brookdale board has already decided how it will vote next month
why: Budget size is not part of the return-rate argument. The Lakeview numbers are about whether books come back, not about money.
The type of item is never discussed. The argument needs the two libraries' borrowers to act alike, not a particular kind of book.
If the board had already decided, the op-ed would be pointless. The argument does not depend on this.

items.skill: Evaluating an argument as a whole
items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates the support in the letter as a whole?
items.hint: Make two lists: sound evidence in the letter and faulty reasoning in the letter. Which list is longer?
items.explain:
Step 1. List the sound support: the parks department's cost estimate (paragraph 2) and the writer's observation of families using the lawn (paragraph 4). Both are relevant.

Step 2. List the faulty reasoning: two littering teenagers (hasty generalization), Cedar Hills break-ins (false cause), lights then a snack stand then pavement (slippery slope), newcomers who “do not understand” (attack on the person), everyone on the writer's street (bandwagon), and skate park or potholes (either-or).

Step 3. So the letter has some relevant evidence but relies mostly on faulty reasoning. The thirty-one-years choice is tempting because experience sounds like expertise, but experience does not turn flawed reasoning into proof.
options: It offers some relevant evidence, such as the cost estimate, but leans heavily on faulty reasoning.
It is well supported, because the writer has lived across from the park for thirty-one years and knows it best.
It is poorly supported, because the writer never gives a single number or names a single source for any point.
It is well supported, because the writer states the skate park supporters' strongest reasons and answers each one.
why: Long experience makes the writer's observations believable, but it cannot fix the hasty generalization, false cause, slippery slope, attack on the person, and either-or in the letter.
This is distorted. The writer does give numbers from a named source: the parks department's estimate of $310,000 to build and $12,000 a year.
The writer never states the supporters' reasons at all. Paragraph 5 attacks the supporters as newcomers instead of answering their reasons.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the author's claim in the op-ed?
items.hint: What does the author want the council to do? Check the end of paragraph 1 and the last paragraph.
items.explain:
Step 1. A claim is what the author wants readers to believe or do. Paragraph 1 says, “The council should approve it,” referring to the proposal to drop the fee for ages 13 to 18. Paragraph 6 repeats, “The council should vote yes.”

Step 2. Ending the $5 fee for teens matches. Correct.

Step 3. The Millbrook visit numbers are evidence. “Teens will not respect a place they do not pay for” is the counterclaim. Hiring coaches is never mentioned.
options: The city council should end the $5 visit fee at the recreation center for residents ages 13 to 18.
At the Millbrook Community Center, average daily teen visits rose from 45 to 120 after the fee ended.
Teens will not respect a recreation center they do not have to pay anything to use.
The city should hire more volunteer coaches so teens have more to do in the afternoons.
why: This is evidence from paragraph 2. It supports the claim, but it is not what the author wants the council to do.
This is the counterclaim from paragraph 2, the worry of some council members that the author argues against.
The author never proposes hiring coaches. He is a volunteer coach, but his claim is about the fee.

items.prompt: What kind of evidence does the author use in paragraph 2 to respond to the worry that damage to the building will rise?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 2. Where do its numbers come from, and what do they compare?
items.explain:
Step 1. Paragraph 2 reports that Millbrook staff logged 14 damage reports in the two years before the fee ended and 13 in the two years after.

Step 2. That is a comparable case: records from another city's center, before and after the same kind of change. Correct.

Step 3. The ninth grader, the sheriff's data, and the petition all appear later in the op-ed and support other points.
options: Records from another city's center comparing damage reports before and after it ended its fee
A personal story about a ninth grader who stopped coming to the center
A statement from the county sheriff's office about the hours when many juvenile arrests happen
A petition signed by people at a youth basketball tournament
why: The ninth grader's story is in paragraph 4 and shows who the fee keeps out. It is not about damage.
The sheriff's data is in paragraph 4 and is about after-school hours, not damage to buildings.
The petition is in paragraph 5 and is about public opinion, not damage.

items.prompt: The author claims that ending the teen fee would cost the city little. Which two details best support this part of his argument? Select two answers.
items.hint: The question is about money. Which details mention dollars the city would lose or save?
items.explain:
Step 1. The part of the argument is that ending the fee would cost the city little, so relevant evidence must be about money.

Step 2. The fees are about 1 percent of the budget ($18,400 ÷ $1,900,000 ≈ 0.97 percent). Correct. And about $11,000 of that is spent collecting it, so the city would lose only about $18,400 − $11,000 = $7,400 a year. Correct.

Step 3. The other details are real evidence from the op-ed, but they support other points: more visits, little damage, safe after-school hours, and public opinion.
options: Teen fees brought in $18,400 last year, about 1 percent of the center's $1.9 million budget.
The center pays a cashier about $11,000 a year, mostly to collect teen fees, a cost that would end.
Average daily teen visits at Millbrook rose from 45 to 120 after its fee ended.
Millbrook staff logged 14 damage reports before the change and 13 after it.
More than a third of juvenile arrests in the county happen between 3 and 7 p.m. on school days.
Three hundred people signed a petition asking the council to make the center free for teens.
why: This supports the point that free entry brings more teens in. It says nothing about money.
This answers the worry about damage. It is not about what the fee earns or costs.
This supports the point about a safe place after school, not the cost to the city.
This is about public opinion, not cost (and it is weak evidence besides).

items.prompt: How does the author respond to the counterclaim that teens will not respect a free center and that damage will rise?
items.hint: Find the paragraph where the counterclaim appears. What does the author say right after it?
items.explain:
Step 1. The counterclaim opens paragraph 2: some council members argue that teens will not respect a free place and that damage will rise.

Step 2. The next sentences are the rebuttal: “That worry is understandable, but the record of a nearby city does not support it,” followed by Millbrook's damage reports (14 before, 13 after). Correct.

Step 3. The arrest data appears later and supports another reason. The author never claims all teens are responsible and never attacks the council members.
options: He calls the worry understandable, then shows that damage reports at a center that went free stayed about the same.
He argues that teens should be trusted to behave well because most of them are responsible young adults.
He points out that more than a third of juvenile arrests happen in the hours just after the school day ends.
He suggests that the council members who raise this worry have never coached or worked with teenagers.
why: The author never makes a general argument about teens being responsible. His answer is evidence from Millbrook's damage log.
The arrest data is in paragraph 4 and supports a different point (a safe place after school). It does not answer whether damage would rise.
The author never criticizes the council members personally. That would be an attack on the person, and it is not in the text.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author states that “the public is behind this idea.” Why does the evidence he gives provide weak support for this statement?
items.hint: Think about who was at the tournament and how the signers were chosen.
items.explain:
Step 1. The claim is broad: the public supports the change. The proof is a petition signed at a youth league tournament.

Step 2. People at a youth basketball tournament are likely to be players, families, and coaches who already care about the center, and they chose to sign. That group may not represent the city, so the evidence is not sufficient or reliable for such a broad claim. Correct.

Step 3. The timing is recent, the number is easy to count, and the petition asks the right question.
options: Signers chose to sign at a youth sports tournament, so they may not represent the city.
The petition was signed in March, so it is too old to show what people think about the fee today.
Three hundred signatures is too many to count accurately, so the number is probably exaggerated.
The petition asked about the teen fee rather than asking people about the center's whole budget.
why: March is recent; the vote is next month. Timing is not the problem. The problem is who signed.
Three hundred signatures can easily be counted. The problem is not the count but whether those people represent the city.
Asking about the teen fee is exactly the right question for this claim. The budget is a different issue.

items.prompt: Paragraph 3 of the letter is shown below. Click the sentence that assumes that because one event came after another, the first event caused the second.
items.hint: Find the sentence that draws a conclusion about cause, not the sentence that only reports what happened.
items.explain:
Step 1. The prompt describes false cause: treating “B came after A” as proof that A caused B.

Step 2. “The food trucks obviously drove them out of business” draws that conclusion. The writer gives no evidence about why the two restaurants closed; rent, the economy, or many other causes could explain it. Correct.

Step 3. The fairground sentences are a different flaw (a hasty generalization from one truck), and the first sentence states the paragraph's reason.
spans: Second, food trucks bring trouble.
Last month at the county fair, I saw one truck leave a pile of greasy boxes behind its stand.
If that is how food truck owners treat a fairground, imagine what they will do to our square.
And look at Brentwood.
That city began allowing food trucks downtown in 2021, and the next year two of its restaurants closed.
The food trucks obviously drove them out of business.
items.why: The most common mistake is clicking the sentence about Brentwood allowing trucks in 2021. That sentence only reports the timing of two events. The false cause is the next sentence, which jumps from that timing to “obviously drove them out of business” with no evidence.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the letter criticizes the people who support the food truck plan instead of responding to their reasons?
items.hint: Look for a sentence about the supporters themselves, not about food trucks or the square.
items.explain:
Step 1. An attack on the person judges an idea by criticizing the people who hold it.

Step 2. In paragraph 5, the writer dismisses supporters as out-of-town operators who pay no local property tax. Where someone lives or pays taxes says nothing about whether food trucks would help or hurt the square. Correct.

Step 3. The other sentences are about the issue itself (parking spaces, fire lanes) or restate the writer's request.
options: Most of them are out-of-town operators who have never paid a dollar of property tax here.
Six food trucks would take at least twelve of those spaces around the square.
The fire marshal has also ruled that no vendor may park in the two fire lanes.
I ask the council to keep it that way and vote no on the food truck plan.
why: This is about parking space, part of the issue itself. It is evidence, not a criticism of the supporters.
This reports a rule from the fire marshal. It is about where trucks may park, not about the people behind the plan.
This restates what the writer wants the council to do. It does not mention the supporters.

items.prompt:
Read the draft letter. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): The darkness puts people at risk. {{0}} Seven of those incidents happened between October and February, when it gets dark before 6 p.m.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): Some residents worry that lights would disturb birds and other wildlife along the river. {{1}} a study by the state wildlife agency found that shielded, downward-facing lights had little (C) on birds nesting along rivers.

Paragraph 3, blank (C): …shielded, downward-facing lights had little {{2}} on birds nesting along rivers.
items.hint: For (A), the next sentence says “those incidents.” For (B), the sentence answers a worry. For (C), decide whether a noun or a verb fits after “had little.”
items.explain:
Blank (A). The topic sentence says the darkness puts people at risk, and the following sentence refers to “those incidents,” so the missing sentence must report incidents. The police reports of falls, thefts, or assaults after dark are relevant, specific, and from a checkable source. Correct.

Blank (B). The first sentence is a counterclaim (lights would disturb wildlife). The study answers it, so a contrast transition is needed: “However,” Correct.

Blank (C). After “had little,” the sentence needs a noun. Effect is the noun meaning “result.” “Affect” is usually a verb. Correct.

options: City police received eleven reports of falls, thefts, or assaults on the path after dark last year.
The Riverwalk path was built in 1996 with money from a state parks grant.
A friend of mine says she would never walk on the Riverwalk at night.
Many cities have riverside paths that are popular with joggers and walkers.
why: The path's history is not about danger, and the next sentence refers to “those incidents,” which this sentence never mentions.
This is one person's feeling. It is not measured evidence, and it does not set up “those incidents.”
This is about other cities' paths and popularity, not about danger on the Riverwalk.

options: However,
For example,
Therefore,
Similarly,
why: “For example” would introduce an example of lights disturbing wildlife. The sentence instead answers the worry with contrasting evidence.
“Therefore” signals a conclusion drawn from the worry. The study does not follow from the worry; it pushes back against it.
“Similarly” signals agreement. The study disagrees with the worry, so a contrast word is needed.

options: effect
affect
affected
why: “Affect” is usually a verb (to affect something). After “had little,” the sentence needs a noun: “effect.”
“Affected” is a verb form. “Had little affected” is not grammatical; the sentence needs the noun “effect.”

items.prompt: Which source gives the most credible and relevant evidence about whether the roundabout itself reduced crashes at Main and Third?
items.hint: Use Who, What, When, Why, and remember that the question is about one intersection.
items.explain:
Step 1. The question is about one intersection: did this roundabout reduce crashes at Main and Third? The best source must be credible and about that intersection.

Step 2. Source A compares police crash reports at the intersection for three years before and three years after, and it includes data and methods a reader can check. Total crashes fell from 38 to 21. Correct. (A city reviewing its own project could have a stake in a good result, which is why its published data matter.)

Step 3. Source C is credible but about other places. Source B has a business stake and no data. Source E is a prediction, not a result.
options: Source A, the Carver City Public Works Department's review
Source B, the press release from the construction company
Source C, the journal article on 40 intersections in other states
Source E, the 2015 newspaper article quoting a traffic engineer
why: The company built the roundabout, so it gains if people think it worked (Why), and it gives no data (What).
This is careful research, but Carver City was not studied. It is credible but does not measure what happened at Main and Third.
This quotes a prediction made six years before the roundabout was built. A prediction is not evidence of what happened.

items.prompt: Drag each statement from the letter into the category that best describes its reasoning.
items.hint: Ask of each statement: too few cases? A chain of unproven steps? Only two choices? Or a relevant, checkable fact?
items.explain:
Hasty generalization: one truck at one fair is used to judge how all food truck owners will treat the square.

Slippery slope: six weekend trucks are said to lead to twenty trucks every night, then carnival rides, then a vendor lot, with no evidence for any step.

Either-or: the writer offers only two outcomes, protecting restaurants or a dying downtown, and ignores other possibilities, such as limits on where trucks park or trucks drawing more people to the square.

Reasonable support: the parking study is a named, official count that is relevant to whether there is room, and the fire marshal's ruling is a checkable official rule about the same question.
choices: Last month at the county fair, I saw one truck leave a pile of greasy boxes behind its stand. If that is how food truck owners treat a fairground, imagine what they will do to our square.
If we allow six trucks on weekends this year, next year there will be twenty trucks every night, then carnival rides, and before long the square will be nothing but a lot for traveling vendors.
Either it protects the restaurants that have served this town for decades, or it watches downtown die.
The city's own parking study counted 84 spaces around the square and found that on Friday evenings, an average of 79 are already filled.
The fire marshal has also ruled that no vendor may park in the two fire lanes on the north side of the square.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the fire marshal's ruling under a fallacy because it helps the writer's side. Helping one side is not a flaw: the ruling is a checkable fact from an official, and it is relevant to whether there is room for trucks.

items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Sources B and D as evidence for the student's question?
items.hint: Check two things for each source: Is it trustworthy? Is it about crashes at Main and Third after 2021?
items.explain:
Step 1: Source B. The construction company built the roundabout, so it gains if people believe it worked (Why), and it gives no numbers (What). It is not reliable.

Step 2: Source D. One driver finds the roundabout confusing. Confusion is not the same as crashes, and one person's view is not sufficient.

Step 3. So neither source answers whether crashes went down. Correct. The “impossible to judge” choice is tempting because the two sources clash, but Source A answers the question with measured crash data.
options: Source B comes from a company with a stake in the project and gives no data, and Source D is one driver's complaint about confusion, not crash records, so neither answers the question well.
Source B is the most reliable source because the company that built the roundabout knows its design best, while Source D proves that the roundabout made the intersection less safe.
Source D is more credible than Source B because it was written two years later, so the student should trust the driver's view over the company's view of the results.
Sources B and D disagree with each other, so the student should treat the roundabout's effect on crashes as impossible to judge from any of the sources.
why: Building the roundabout gives the company a reason to praise it (Why), and it offers no data. Source D describes confusion, not crashes, so it proves nothing about safety.
Being written later does not make a source more credible. Source D is still one person's opinion about confusion, with no crash data.
Two weak sources disagreeing does not make the question impossible. Source A has measured crash data that answers it directly.

items.prompt: Return to the op-ed about the recreation center. Which statement, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?
items.hint: Which piece of evidence depends on an assumption about cause? What new fact could offer another cause?
items.explain:
Step 1. A central reason is that free entry would bring more teens through the doors. The key evidence is Millbrook, where daily teen visits rose from 45 to 120 after its fee ended. The argument assumes the end of the fee caused that rise.

Step 2. If Millbrook opened a new gym and began free meals the same year, those changes could explain the rise in visits. That breaks the assumed cause-and-effect link. Correct.

Step 3. The arrest data already appears in the op-ed and supports the author. The library fact is about a different service. A growing budget makes the lost fee money matter less, which helps the author.
options: In the same year Millbrook ended its teen fee, it also opened a new gym and began serving free after-school meals.
More than a third of juvenile arrests in the county happen between 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. on school days.
Many public libraries in the state have stopped charging teens for computer use in the past five years.
The Ridgeway center's overall budget has grown by about 3 percent a year over the last decade, mostly from state recreation grants.
why: This fact is already in the op-ed, and it supports the author's point about after-school hours. It cannot weaken his argument.
Libraries and computer fees are a different service. This says nothing about whether ending the center's fee would bring in more teens.
A growing budget does not weaken the argument. If anything, it makes the loss of $18,400 in fees matter even less.

items.skill: Writing a sound argument; relevant evidence
items.prompt:
Read the draft letter again. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 5, blank (D): The writer wants a closing sentence that restates the claim without faulty reasoning. {{0}} Please light the Riverwalk before another winter comes.

The writer's strongest evidence that the path is dangerous is {{1}}.
items.hint: For (D), ask whether each choice gives a reason or attacks, predicts disaster, or follows the crowd. For the second blank, ask which detail actually measures danger.
items.explain:
Blank (D). A sound closing restates the claim and the main reasons: lights would make the path safer for its many users at a modest cost. The other three choices are faulty reasoning: an attack on the person, a slippery slope, and a bandwagon appeal.

Second blank. The claim is that the path is dangerous, so the strongest evidence is a reliable record of harm on the path: eleven police reports after dark last year. The number of users is tempting because it shows many people are affected, but it does not measure danger.

options: Lights would make the path safer for the hundreds of people who use it, at a modest cost to the city.
Anyone who votes against this plan clearly does not care whether people get hurt in the dark.
If the council does nothing, soon no one in this city will dare to walk anywhere after dark.
Every city worth living in already has bright lights along all of its river paths.
why: This attacks the people who might vote no instead of answering their reasons. It is an attack on the person.
This is a slippery slope: it jumps from one dark path to no one walking anywhere, with no evidence.
This is a bandwagon appeal with loaded language (“worth living in”). It gives no evidence.

options: the police reports of falls, thefts, and assaults on the path after dark
the wildlife agency's study of shielded, downward-facing lights
the engineering office's estimate that the lights would cost $160,000
the number of people who walk the path to the train or night classes
why: This answers the wildlife counterclaim in paragraph 3. It says nothing about danger to people.
This supports the point that the project is affordable. It does not show danger.
This shows heavy use, which matters, but heavy use alone does not prove danger. Incident reports do.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the op-ed on the recreation center.

The author's story in paragraph 4 about the ninth grader is {{0}}. The sheriff's data in paragraph 4 supports the claim only if the reader assumes that {{1}}.
items.hint: For the first blank, use the three evidence tests. For the second, ask what must be true for arrest timing to prove that a free center helps.
items.explain:
First blank. The story is relevant and easy to picture, but it is one teen. It is not sufficient to show how many teens the fee keeps away.

Second blank. The sheriff's data shows that many juvenile arrests happen after school. It supports a free center only if teens at the center would be less likely to get into trouble than they would be elsewhere. That is the unstated assumption. The weekend choice is tempting because it mentions timing, but it contradicts the data rather than linking it to the claim.

options: moving, but one teen's experience cannot show how many teens the fee keeps away
the strongest evidence in the op-ed, because the author knows the teen personally
irrelevant, because it is about a teen who no longer uses the center
the counterclaim, which the author answers in the following paragraph
why: Knowing the teen makes the story believable and vivid, not sufficient. One case cannot show how common the problem is.
It is relevant: the claim is that the fee keeps teens away, and this teen stopped coming because of it. Its weakness is size, not relevance.
The counterclaim is in paragraph 2 (teens will not respect a free center). The story supports the author's own position.

options: teens at the center after school would be less likely to get into trouble than they would be elsewhere
the sheriff's office makes more arrests in the county than any other police agency does
most juvenile arrests in the county happen on weekends rather than on school days
the Ridgeway center charges a higher fee than the Millbrook center charged
why: Which agency makes the most arrests is not part of the argument. The data matters only if the center would keep teens out of trouble.
This contradicts the sheriff's data, which says many arrests happen on school-day afternoons. The argument does not need it.
The size of the fee is not connected to the arrest data. The argument needs the center to be a safer place for teens.

items.skill: Evaluating an argument as a whole
items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates the support in the letter as a whole?
items.hint: Make two lists: sound evidence and faulty reasoning. Then ask Who and Why about the writer.
items.explain:
Step 1. Sound support: the city's parking study and the fire marshal's ruling (paragraph 2). Both are relevant and checkable.

Step 2. Faulty reasoning: one truck at a fair (hasty generalization), Brentwood's restaurant closings (false cause), twenty trucks then carnival rides (slippery slope), out-of-town operators (attack on the person), every customer at the diner (bandwagon, from a one-sided group), and protect restaurants or watch downtown die (either-or).

Step 3. The writer also owns a diner on the square, so she has a business reason (Why) to keep competitors away. That does not make her wrong, but it is a reason to look hard at her evidence. The nineteen-years choice is tempting, but experience does not turn flawed reasoning into proof.
options: It has relevant parking evidence but leans on faulty reasoning, and the writer competes with trucks.
It is well supported, because a diner owner of nineteen years understands the square better than anyone else does.
It is poorly supported, because the writer never names an official source or gives a number for any point at all.
It is well supported, because the writer fairly states the food truck supporters' reasons and then answers each one.
why: Long experience makes the writer's observations believable, but it cannot fix the hasty generalization, false cause, slippery slope, attack on the person, and either-or in the letter. The writer also has a business stake.
This is distorted. The writer cites the city's parking study (84 spaces, 79 filled) and the fire marshal's ruling.
The writer never states the supporters' reasons. Paragraph 5 attacks the supporters as out-of-town operators instead of answering them.

stimuli.title: Evening Classes Belong at the Library
stimuli.html:
An opinion column by Renata Cole, a member of the Harlan County Library board

(1) Harlan County offers free GED preparation classes, but only on weekday mornings at the county office building downtown. For adults who work during the day, those classes might as well not exist. The county should move half of its GED classes to weekday evenings and hold them at its four branch libraries.

(2) The need is real. The county's adult education office reports that 260 people asked about GED classes last year, and 41 percent of them said they could not attend morning classes because of work. The branch libraries are also closer to where people live. According to the county planning department, nine in ten residents live within three miles of a branch, while the county office building is a forty-minute bus ride from the east side.

(3) Some people argue that evening classes will cost too much because the libraries would have to stay open later. But all four branches are already open until 8 p.m. on weeknights, and the library director says the classes could use meeting rooms that sit empty most evenings.

(4) Moving the classes will also change lives. Last year my neighbor finally earned his diploma after three tries, and he now supervises a warehouse crew. If the county does not act, more people like him will give up, and soon our whole workforce will fall behind every county around us.

(5) The county board should vote to bring GED classes to the libraries this fall.

stimuli.title: Sources on Dawson County's Evening Classes
stimuli.html:
A student is researching this question: Did Dawson County's switch to evening GED classes in 2023 increase the number of adults who enrolled?

SourceWhat it is
1Dawson County adult education office, annual report, 2025. Gives enrollment for each year from 2020 to 2024 and explains how students were counted. Average yearly enrollment: 112 before the switch, 187 after.

stimuli.title: Take the Clinic to the Market
stimuli.html:
An opinion column by Dr. Alan Pierce, a family doctor in Westfield County

(1) Westfield County's free blood pressure and diabetes screenings take place only at the county health department, on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Many working residents never make it there. The health department should also hold free screenings at the Saturday farmers market from May through October.

(2) Many residents who need these screenings are not getting them. The health department's own records show that only 2,100 people were screened last year in a county of about 48,000 adults. According to the state health survey, about one in four adults in the county has high blood pressure.

(3) The market is where people already are. The market association counts an average of 3,400 shoppers each Saturday, and the market sits one block from the county's main bus stop.

(4) Some worry that a busy outdoor market is the wrong place for private health questions. However, the health department already runs screenings at the county fair inside a closed tent, and the nurses who work there report no complaints about privacy.

(5) This idea is too important to wait. Everyone I know at my church thinks it is a great plan. And anyone who opposes it simply does not care about the health of working families.

(6) The health department should set up its tent at the market this May.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the author's claim?
items.explain: The author states what she wants at the end of paragraph 1 (“The county should move half of its GED classes to weekday evenings and hold them at its four branch libraries”) and repeats it in paragraph 5. The 41 percent figure is tempting because it is a key number, but it is evidence for the claim, not the claim itself.
options: The county should move half of its GED classes to evenings and hold them at the branch libraries.
Forty-one percent of the people who asked about GED classes could not attend in the morning.
Evening GED classes will cost the county too much because the libraries would stay open later.
Earning a GED can lead adults to better-paying jobs, such as supervising a warehouse crew for a company.
why: This is evidence from paragraph 2. It supports the claim, but it is not what the author wants the county to do.
This is the counterclaim from paragraph 3, the view the author argues against.
This comes from the neighbor's story in paragraph 4. It is a detail, and the author never makes this general claim about jobs.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 is shown below. Click the sentence that claims, without evidence, that one decision will lead to a chain of worse and worse results.
items.explain: The final sentence jumps from one decision (not moving the classes) to people giving up and then to the whole county's workforce falling behind, with no evidence for any step. That is a slippery slope. The neighbor's story is a different weakness: one case cannot show how many people would benefit.
spans: Moving the classes will also change lives.
Last year my neighbor finally earned his diploma after three tries, and he now supervises a warehouse crew.
If the county does not act, more people like him will give up, and soon our whole workforce will fall behind every county around us.
items.why: Students often click the neighbor's story because it is weak evidence. It is an anecdote, not a chain of predictions. The slippery slope is the sentence that leaps from not moving classes to the whole workforce falling behind.

items.prompt: Which detail best supports the author's point that the libraries would be easier for students to reach?
items.explain: The point is about getting there. The planning department's figure that nine in ten residents live within three miles of a branch directly shows the libraries are close. The weeknight hours are tempting because they make the libraries available, but they are about cost and timing, not about distance.
options: Nine in ten residents live within three miles of a branch library.
All four branch libraries are already open until 8 p.m. on weeknights.
Some library meeting rooms sit empty on most weeknight evenings.
Last year 260 people asked the county about its GED classes.
why: This shows the libraries are open in the evening, which answers the cost worry. It says nothing about distance from people's homes.
Empty rooms show there is space for classes. They do not show that the libraries are close to where people live.
This shows interest in classes, not how easy the libraries are to reach.

items.prompt: Which two pieces of support in the op-ed are the weakest? Select two answers.
items.explain: The neighbor's story is one case; it is vivid but not sufficient to show how many people evening classes would help. The workforce prediction is a slippery slope with no evidence for any step. The other choices come from named county sources or checkable facts and are relevant to the claim.
options: The county adult education office reports that 41 percent of 260 people could not attend morning classes because of work.
The county planning department reports that nine in ten residents live within three miles of a branch library.
All four branch libraries are already open until 8 p.m. on weeknights.
The author's neighbor earned his diploma after three tries and now supervises a warehouse crew.
If the county does not act, soon the whole workforce will fall behind every county around it.
why: This is a figure from a named county office, and it is directly relevant: it shows many people cannot attend morning classes. It is strong support.
This is a figure from the county planning department, relevant to whether residents could reach the classes. It is strong support.
This is a checkable fact about library hours, and it directly answers the cost worry. It is strong support.

items.prompt: How does the author respond to the concern that evening classes will cost too much?
items.explain: The counterclaim is in paragraph 3: evening classes would cost too much because the libraries would have to stay open later. The rebuttal follows “But”: the branches are already open until 8 p.m., and the classes could use empty meeting rooms, so no extra hours are needed. The life-changing choice is tempting because paragraph 4 talks about changed lives, but that paragraph never mentions cost.
options: She shows that the branches are already open until 8 p.m. and have meeting rooms that sit empty.
She argues that the cost does not matter because a GED changes a person's life for the better.
She points out that the county office building is a forty-minute bus ride from the east side.
She suggests that the people who worry about cost do not understand the needs of working adults.
why: The author does not dismiss the cost. She answers it with facts about current library hours and empty rooms.
The bus ride supports the point that the libraries are easier to reach. It does not answer the cost worry.
The author never criticizes the people who raise the concern. That would be an attack on the person.

items.explain: Paragraph 3 begins, “Some people argue that evening classes will cost too much,” which is the counterclaim. The next sentence, beginning “But,” answers it. Answer: 3.

Source 1 gives yearly enrollment before and after the switch, from the office that runs the classes, and explains its counting method (Who, What, When). Average enrollment rose from 112 to 187. Source 2, the blog post by the online GED course company
Source 3, the minutes of the 2021 county board meeting
Source 4, the national survey of 5,000 adults without diplomas
why: The company sells online courses, so it gains if readers doubt evening classes (Why), and it gives no data about Dawson County.

Complete the statement about the op-ed “Evening Classes Belong at the Library.”

The adult education office's figure that 41 percent could not attend morning classes supports the claim only if the reader assumes that {{0}}. The argument would be most weakened if it turned out that {{1}}.
items.explain:
First blank. The figure shows that many people cannot come in the morning. It supports evening classes only if those people could come in the evening. That is the unstated assumption.

Second blank. If most of those working adults also could not come in the evening, the assumption breaks and the evidence no longer supports the claim. The parking choice is tempting because it is about the libraries, but it helps the argument.

options: many of those people could attend classes in the evening
the county office building is too small for GED classes
GED classes are more useful than other adult classes
why: The size of the building is never discussed. The figure matters only if people who miss morning classes could come at night.

options: most of those working adults also could not attend evening classes because of child care
the branch libraries have more free parking than the county office building
the county has offered free GED classes at its office building since 1998
why: More parking would make the libraries easier to use. That strengthens the argument rather than weakening it.

About one in four adults in Westfield County has high blood pressure, according to the state health survey.
A busy outdoor market is the wrong place for residents to ask nurses private health questions.
The farmers market should move closer to the county's main bus stop so more shoppers can reach it.

That is an attack on the person. The church sentence is a different flaw: a bandwagon appeal based on a small, likeminded group.

Everyone I know at my church thinks it is a great plan.
And anyone who opposes it simply does not care about the health of working families.

The 2,100-screened figure is tempting because it is about screenings, but it supports the point that a need exists, not that people are at the market.
options: The market association counts an average of 3,400 shoppers each Saturday.
Only 2,100 people were screened last year in a county of about 48,000 adults.
Nurses at the county fair tent report no complaints about privacy.
About one in four adults in the county has high blood pressure.
why: This shows that few people are being screened now. It does not show that people are at the market.
This answers the privacy worry. It says nothing about how many people go to the market.

items.explain: The church comment is a bandwagon appeal from a small group that may share the author's views; it is not sufficient to show public support. The statement about opponents is an attack on the person and offers no evidence at all. The other choices come from named sources and are relevant to the claim.
options: The health department's records show that only 2,100 people were screened last year in a county of about 48,000 adults.

The market association counts an average of 3,400 shoppers each Saturday at the farmers market.
Everyone the author knows at his church thinks the plan is a great idea.
Anyone who opposes the plan simply does not care about the health of working families.
why: This comes from the health department's own records and shows how few people are screened. It is strong, relevant support.
This is a figure from a state survey that shows a real health need. It is strong support.
This is a count from the market association, relevant to whether people are at the market. It is strong support.

items.prompt: How does the author respond to the concern that a busy market is the wrong place for private health questions?

The rebuttal follows “However”: the health department already screens people inside a closed tent at the county fair, and nurses report no privacy complaints. The “do not care” choice is tempting because those words appear in the op-ed, but that sentence is an attack on the person in paragraph 5, not the answer to the privacy concern.
options: He points to screenings in a closed tent at the county fair, where nurses report no privacy complaints.
He argues that privacy matters less than health, so residents should accept less privacy at the market.
He notes that the market is only one block from the county's main bus stop, so it is easy to reach.
He suggests that the people who raise this worry do not care about the health of working families.

The bus stop supports the point that people can reach the market. It does not answer the privacy worry.
This sentence is in paragraph 5 and is aimed at anyone who opposes the plan. The author's actual answer to the privacy worry, in paragraph 4, is the fair-tent evidence.

items.explain: Paragraph 4 begins, “Some worry that a busy outdoor market is the wrong place for private health questions,” which is the counterclaim. The next sentence, beginning “However,” answers it. Answer: 4.

mistakes.why: Paragraph 5 mentions people who oppose the plan, but it attacks them instead of stating and answering their view.

Source 3 gives yearly counts before and after, from the department that runs the screenings, and explains how people were counted. The average rose from 3,900 to 6,200. The journal study is tempting because it is peer-reviewed research, but it is about other counties.

Complete the statement about the op-ed “Take the Clinic to the Market.”

The market's count of 3,400 Saturday shoppers supports the claim only if the reader assumes that {{0}}. The argument would be most weakened if it turned out that {{1}}.
items.explain:
First blank. A crowd at the market supports the plan only if many of those shoppers would stop to be screened. That is the unstated assumption.

Second blank. If most market shoppers already get regular checkups, the screenings would mostly reach people who are not missing care, and the argument that the market reaches unscreened residents falls apart. The vendor-booth choice is tempting because it is about the market, but it does not touch the assumption.

the farmers market is larger than the county fair
screenings cost less at a market than at the health department

the market association added twenty new vendor booths over the last five years

vocab.def: A piece of writing or speech that tries to convince the reader to believe or do something.
vocab.example: A letter urging the council to build a new bus shelter.

vocab.def: The main position an author wants readers to accept; something reasonable people could disagree about.
vocab.example: The library should stop charging late fines.

vocab.def: Facts, statistics, research, expert statements, or examples used to support a claim.
vocab.example: Fines brought in $21,500, less than 1 percent of the budget.

vocab.def: The logic that explains how the evidence proves the claim.
vocab.example: Return rates stayed the same without fines, so fines are not what gets books returned.

vocab.def: An idea the author takes for granted without stating it, which the argument depends on.
vocab.example: Assuming our town will respond the same way a nearby town did.

vocab.def: A position that opposes the author's claim.
The author's response that answers or disproves a counterclaim.
vocab.example: But return rates barely changed when another library dropped fines.

vocab.def: Evidence that is directly connected to the claim it is meant to support.
vocab.example: Crash data from the street in question, not from a different city.

vocab.def: Enough evidence to support the size of the claim being made.
vocab.example: One story is not sufficient to describe a whole town.

vocab.def: How trustworthy and believable a source is, based on its expertise, evidence, date, and purpose.
vocab.example: A peer-reviewed study is usually more credible than an online comment.

vocab.def: A leaning toward one side, often because the author has something to gain or a strong personal view.
vocab.example: A shop owner praising a project that brings customers to the shop.

vocab.def: A flaw in logic that makes an argument seem stronger than it really is.
vocab.example: Insulting the other side instead of answering it.

vocab.def: A broad conclusion drawn from too few examples.
vocab.example: Two teens littered, so all skaters will ruin the park.

vocab.def: Assuming that because one event followed another, the first event caused the second.
vocab.example: Break-ins rose after the skate park opened, so the skate park caused them.

vocab.def: Claiming, without proof, that one step will lead to a chain of increasingly bad results.
vocab.example: Allow a skate park, and soon the whole park will be paved.

notes:
Week 5 RLA Study Sheet: Analyzing Arguments

Parts of an argument

  • Claim: what the author wants you to believe or do
  • Reason: why the author thinks so
  • Evidence: facts, numbers, studies, expert statements, examples
  • Reasoning: how the evidence proves the claim
  • Assumption: an unstated link the author needs you to accept
  • Counterclaim: the other side's view
  • Rebuttal: the author's answer to it

Three tests for evidence

  1. Relevant: about this claim?
  2. Sufficient: enough to cover the claim?
  3. Reliable: trustworthy, fairly gathered, checkable?

Strongest: data from a named, fair source. Weakest: one story, a self-selected poll, “everyone knows.”

Source credibility

  • Who: expertise?
  • What: data and methods, or opinion?
  • When: current for this question?
  • Why: does the author gain if you agree?

Credible is not the same as relevant. Check both.

Find the assumption

Ask: what must be true for this evidence to prove this claim? Common one: “it worked there, so it will work here.”

Strengthen or weaken?

Strengthens: supports the assumption. Weakens: breaks it, often with another cause or a key difference.

Faulty reasoning

TypeSignAsk yourself
Hasty generalizationBig conclusion, few casesEnough examples?
False causeB came after A, so A caused BOther explanations?
Slippery slopeOne step leads to disasterIs each step proven?
Either-orOnly two choicesOther options?
Attack on the personInsults the arguerWere the reasons answered?
BandwagonEveryone thinks soPopular = proven?
Straw manTwists the other side's viewDid they really say that?
Appeal to emotionFeelings replace factsWhat proof is left?

Strategy: Set your opinion aside. Find the claim, then point to the proof for each answer choice.

Common mistakes: calling a statistic the claim; trusting any number; choosing the side you agree with; trusting a credible but off-topic source.
